<!-- head-1: body_md -->
The context in which our setup takes place is the cohesive $\infty$-topos of smooth $\infty$-groupoids (cf. Definition~\ref{app:def:cohesive})
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{H}:= {\rm Sh}\left({\rm CartSp},\infty{\rm Grpd}\right),
\end{equation}
modeled as a topos of sheaves on the site of Cartesian spaces valued in $\infty$-groupoids. We will interchangeably refer to these as higher smooth stacks. By definition as sheaves, any object $\mathcal{X} \in {\rm ob}\,\textbf{H}$ can be evaluated at a Cartesian space $U\in {\rm ob\, CartSp}$, naturally yielding an $\infty$-groupoid $\mathcal{X}(U)\in {\rm ob\, \infty Grpd}$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rmk:-1-formsymmetries}
We highlight that this definition of electric global symmetries includes only symmetries of non-negative degree. Nowadays, it is common to speak of \textit{$(-1)$-form symmetries}, which are associated with \textit{families} of theories. The setting of \cite{Perez-Lona:2025xxm} summarized here, by contrast, focuses on a single theory, namely an $\mathcal{X}$-valued $\sigma$-model. In our study of magnetic symmetries in the present article, we will however see the emergence of $(-1)$-form symmetry backgrounds.

Extending the present framework to include electric global symmetries of degree $k\geq -1$ is straightforward, but since we will not need this here, we only describe it briefly as follows: it amounts to passing from group object actions to group\textit{oid} object actions, as recognized from a different perspective in \cite[Example 1.4]{Stockall:2025ngz}. In our setting, the role of the acting group object, realized as a simplicial object $(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G})_{\bullet}$ (Definition~\ref{app:def:gp-obj}), is replaced by a groupoid object $(\mathscr{G})_{\bullet}$ (Definition~\ref{app:def:groupoid-object}). The action groupoid $(\mathcal{X} 
  \IfBooleanTF{#1}
    {\big/\mkern-7mu\big/}
    {/\mkern-6mu/}
 \mathscr{G})_{\bullet}$, encoding the action, is adjusted appropriately: since $(\mathscr{G})_{0} = \mathscr{G}_0 \in \mathrm{ob}\, \textbf{H}$ is not the terminal object anymore, a $\mathscr{G}$-action on $\mathcal{X}$ now features a map valued in $\mathscr{G}_0$. This is the familiar \textit{anchor map} of groupoid actions (e.g. \cite[Section 1]{Mackenzie2005}).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rmk:electric-flat-comodal}
  We emphasize that electric symmetries \eqref{eq:electric-g-symmetry-homomorphism} are defined as actions of a group object in \textbf{H} that is \textit{discrete}, equivalently $\flat$-\textit{comodal}, meaning there is an equivalence
  \begin{equation}
      {\sf G} \cong \flat {\sf G}
  \end{equation}
  between $\sf G$ and its image under the $\flat$-comodality of \textbf{H}. This is because, since the group acts via flat maps, its action, and hence the field theory, cannot distinguish any smooth structure. This will play an important role in Section~\ref{ssec:magnetic-cosymmetries}, where it is
the discreteness of $\sf G$ that places electric symmetries and magnetic co-symmetries on
the two sides of the adjunction $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\dashv\flat$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rmk:terminal-electric}
  A clear way to characterize the universal property \eqref{eq:electric-symmetry-diagram} satisfied by $\flat {\rm Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ is that it is the \textit{terminal} object in the category of \textit{discrete group actions} on $\mathcal{X}$. The objects in this category are pairs $(\mathsf G,\rho:\mathsf{G}\times \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X})$, where $\mathsf G$ is a discrete group object and $\rho$ is a group action, and morphisms are stacky group homomorphisms compatible with the actions.

  Incidentally, the condition that a map of stacks \eqref{eq:electric-g-symmetry-homomorphism} is a homomorphism of stacky groups is equivalent to requiring that the map admits a \textit{delooping}
    \begin{equation}
        \rho: \mathbf{B}\mathsf{G} \to \mathbf{B}\flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \cong \flat \mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}).
    \end{equation}
    Since in this presentation the coherence data is automatically taken care of, we will switch between these two presentations when needed.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:mch} Let $\Sigma \to \mathcal{X}$ be a $\sigma$-model. We call the collection of maps
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-mch}
    \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,{\cal X}):= [\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
{\cal X}]
\end{equation}
the stack of \textit{magnetic charges} (cf.\ the treatment of charge sectors via shapes of classifying spaces in \cite{Sati:2023mta}).
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:mch-shape-fields}
Let $\Sigma$ be a smooth manifold. The map \eqref{eq:fields-to-mch} is the $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-unit of $\textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$, so that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mch-shape-fields}
    
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\,\textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})\cong\textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The smooth Oka principle \cite[Theorem 4.3.54(i)]{Sati_Schreiber_2026} gives $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
[\Sigma,\mathcal{X}]\cong[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}]$. Since $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$ is discrete, and $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$ preserves finite products with $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 U\cong *$ for every Cartesian space $U$, both $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}]$ and $[\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}]$ have $U$-points $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X})$, hence $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}]\cong[\Sigma,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}]$. In particular, $\textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ is discrete, and the composite equivalence is the map induced by \eqref{eq:fields-to-mch} through the $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-unit.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rmk:x-pointed-connected}
    Given that we will always assume $\Sigma$ is path-connected, that ultimately the constructions depend only on how $\Sigma$ maps into the stacks involved, and that $\Sigma$ always lands in a single connected component of the target space, we will assume that the target stack $\mathcal{X}$ is also path-connected, in the appropriate sense for stacks. Technically, this means we assume $\mathcal{X}$ has a single concordance class (cf. \cite[Example 4.3.50]{Sati_Schreiber_2026}):
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:connected-stack}
        \tau_{\leq 0}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} = *,
    \end{equation}
    where $\tau_{\leq 0}$ is the $0$-truncation as in Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncation}.
    For instance, if $\mathcal{X}=X$ is some smooth manifold, the requirement becomes $\tau_{\leq 0}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X = \pi_0(X)=*$. Similarly, for $\mathcal{X}= \mathbf{B}G$ we have $\tau_{\leq 0}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{B}G = \tau_{\leq 0}\mathbf{B}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 G=\pi_0(BG)=*.$

    With this condition, we will also assume an arbitrary choice of basepoint $x: * \to \mathcal{X}$, making $\mathcal{X}$ a \textit{pointed} stack $(\mathcal{X},x)$ (cf. Example~\ref{app:ex:pointed-slice}), and the $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-unit \eqref{eq:shape-unit} a map of pointed stacks.

    Notice that this makes $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ pointed too:
    \begin{equation}
        \eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_{\mathcal{X}} \circ x: * \to \mathcal{X} \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}.
    \end{equation}
    This may be denoted as $\mathsf{x}$ or $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 x$, depending on whether we want to emphasize it is a point of a discrete stack, or that it is the point coming from a $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-unit.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:magnetic-charges-s1} Let $\mathcal{X} = S^1$. This is the target space for many physically relevant theories, notably the two-dimensional compact boson, which we shall analyze in greater detail in the upcoming \cite{PerezLona:applications}. The homotopy type of the circle $S^1$ is well-known: it corresponds to the Eilenberg--MacLane space $K(\mathbb{Z},1)$. However, we will often find explicit path-based presentations more useful in the smooth context than the equivalent but purely topological skeletons. Therefore, \textit{at the level of $1$-groupoids}, we have
\begin{equation}
    {\rm ob}\,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^1 = S^1, \quad {\rm mor}\,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^1 = \mathbb{R}\times S^1.
\end{equation}
Then, choosing a good cover $\{U_i\}_{i\in \mathcal{I}}$ for $\Sigma$, an object in (the global sections of) $\textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,S^1)$ consists of locally constant maps
\begin{equation}
    z_i:U_i \to S^1,\quad x_{ij}:U_{ij} \to \mathbb{R},
\end{equation}
satisfying the condition
\begin{equation}
    z_j = \exp(2\pi \mathrm{i}\,x_{ij})z_i,\quad x_{ik} = x_{ij}+x_{jk}.
\end{equation}  
Similarly, a morphism $y_i:(z_i,x_{ij}) \to (\tilde{z}_i,\tilde{x}_{ij})$ in $\textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,S^1)$ consists of locally constant maps
\begin{equation}
    y_i:U_i \to \mathbb{R},
\end{equation}
such that
\begin{equation}
\tilde{z}_i = \exp(2\pi \mathrm{i}\,y_i)z_i,  \quad y_j + x_{ij} = \tilde{x}_{ij} + y_i.
\end{equation}
Thus, we see that if we pick a basepoint e.g. $z \in S^1$, any object $(z_i,x_{ij})$ is isomorphic to an object of the form $(z_i=z,m_{ij}\in \mathbb{Z})$, that is, a principal $\mathbb{Z}$-bundle, as expected. Note that we have not used the fact that $S^1$ can be equipped with a group structure, only that it has a translation action by the additive group $\mathbb{R}$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{X} = \mathbf{B}_{\nabla}U(1)$ be the moduli stack of principal $U(1)$-bundles with connection, which we take to be the gauge fields of Maxwell theory. This can be understood as the first categorification of Example~\ref{ex:magnetic-charges-s1}. The magnetic charges are then
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) = \left[\Sigma, 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{B}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]= \left[\Sigma, \mathbf{B}^2\mathbb{Z}\right].
\end{equation}
This describes ordinary integral cohomology on $\Sigma$, and physically these are the Dirac charge-quantized magnetic charges for Maxwell theory.

One should keep in mind the terminology issue highlighted in Footnote~\ref{footnote:topological-vs-magnetic} in Section~\ref{sec:intro}, i.e. that what is physically speaking labeled as the ``magnetic charges'' of a theory depends on the choice of quantization. As mentioned in said footnote, the Freed--Moore--Segal \cite[Section 1]{Freed:2006ya} quantization proposal for Maxwell theory lets $\mathbf{B}^2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbf{B}^2\mathbb{Z}$ be the classifying space for electric and magnetic fluxes. For this proposal, our Definition~\ref{def:mch} gives the mapping higher groupoid $[\Sigma, \mathbf{B}^2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbf{B}^2\mathbb{Z}]$ as the higher groupoid of ``magnetic charges'', though physically these include both electric and magnetic charges. Hence, strictly speaking, what \eqref{eq:def-mch} encodes are \textit{topological} charges, but due to the electric/magnetic duality picture the term evokes, which is central to our framework in the precise form of the op-duality between electric symmetries and magnetic co-symmetries established below, we will keep using the widely-used term ``magnetic charges'' despite the unfortunate clash.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
Mathematically, magnetic co-symmetries are \textit{nonabelian cohomology operations} (see \cite[Section 2]{Fiorenza:2020dcp}).
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
We will mostly assume $\mathsf{Y}$ is of the form $\mathsf{Y} = \mathbf{B}\mathsf{G}$ for $\mathsf{G}$ some $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-modal group object in \textbf{H}. This is a consequence of requiring $\sf Y$ to be path-connected, $\tau_{\leq 0}\mathsf{Y} = *$. The point $\mathsf{y}$ is thus the essentially unique point $\bullet$ of $\mathbf{B}\mathsf{G}$. This assumption allows us to keep a clear parallel with electric symmetries of non-negative degree. We nevertheless formulate our framework in terms of pointed path-connected stacks (in the sense of \eqref{eq:connected-stack}) without appealing to the equivalent presentation as a delooping of a discrete $\infty$-group. Thus, a choice of basepoint is necessary but can be arbitrary.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rmk:pointed-co-monoids}
In the pointed setting $\mathbf H_{*/}$ with the smash product, co-monoid structures are no longer automatic. The reduced diagonal $\mathcal Y\to\mathcal Y\wedge\mathcal Y$ exists, but for $\mathcal Y$ connected the only pointed map $\mathcal Y\to S^0$ to the monoidal unit is null, so no counit is available (the null map fails counitality unless $\mathcal Y\cong *$) and $\mathcal Y$ admits no $\wedge$-co-monoid structure. Objects of the form $\mathcal Y_+$ are co-monoids via the diagonal. Co-$H$-structures, such as those on suspensions, are instead taken with respect to the wedge sum, the coproduct of $\mathbf H_{*/}$. We do not use either here but see Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:postnikov-magnetic-co-symmetries}
A crucial and, in a sense, canonical example of magnetic co-symmetries is given by the \textit{Postnikov tower} of the discrete object $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$. This is a filtration induced by the $n$-truncations $\tau_{\leq n}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ (see Appendix~\ref{app:sec:structures}, cf. Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncation})
\begin{equation}\label{eq:n-truncation-filtration}
    
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to \cdots \to \mathsf{X}_{i+1}\to \mathsf{X}_{i} \to \mathsf{X}_{i-1}\to \cdots \to \mathsf{X}_1 \to \mathsf{X}_0 = \pi_0(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}) \to \mathsf{X}_{-1}=*,
\end{equation}
where we denote $\mathsf{X}_n = \tau_{\leq n} 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$, and the morphisms $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to \mathsf{X}_n$ are $(n+1)$-connected (Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncated-connected-morphism}). Under the assumption of Remark~\ref{rmk:x-pointed-connected}, $\mathsf X_0=*$. These higher groupoids $\mathsf{X}_n$ are discrete. In our conventions, then, the system \eqref{eq:n-truncation-filtration} of higher groupoids describes a system of magnetic co-symmetries $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to \mathsf{X}_n$ which we name \textit{Postnikov magnetic co-symmetries}\footnote{For the case of $\mathcal{X} = X$ a topological space, this filtration of magnetic charges appears in \cite{Sheckler:2025rlk}.}.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:trivially-acting-magnetic-co-symmetry}
Let $\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}: (
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\eta_{\mathcal{X}}^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}\circ x) \to (\mathsf{Y},\mathsf{y})$ be a magnetic co-symmetry. Its \textit{cokernel} is the homotopy pushout in $\textbf{H}_{*/}$
\begin{equation}
    \begin{tikzcd}
    
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X} \arrow[r, "\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}"] \arrow[d] & \mathsf{Y} \arrow[d, "q"] \\
    * \arrow[r, "\mathsf{y}'"'] & \mathsf{C}:=\mathrm{cofib}(\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}})
    \arrow["\ulcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125, rotate=180}, draw=none, from=2-2, to=1-1]
    \end{tikzcd},
\end{equation}
which is again discrete, since $\mathrm{Dsc}$ preserves colimits. We call the composite
\begin{equation}
    q\circ\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}:\ 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X} \longrightarrow \mathsf{C}
\end{equation}
the associated \textit{trivially-co-acting magnetic co-symmetry}. In particular, the pushout square gives a canonical null-homotopy $q\circ\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}\cong(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}\to *\xrightarrow{\mathsf y'}\mathsf C)$, so that the co-action
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{X} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{X}}, \text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}})} \mathcal{X} \times \mathsf{Y} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{X}}\times q} \mathcal{X} \times \mathsf{C}
\end{equation}
factors through $\mathcal{X} \times *$, canonically up to homotopy.
<!-- end definition-3 -->

<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:infty-mcg}
    For $\mathcal{X} \in \mathrm{ob\,}\textbf{H}$, we call the discrete group object $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ the $\infty$\textit{-mapping class group} of $\mathcal{X}$.

    The $\infty$-mapping class group $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 {\rm Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ canonically acts on the shape $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ of $\mathcal{X}$. This follows from applying the result quoted in Remark~\ref{rmk:shape-groupoid} to the canonical evaluation action map $\mathbf{ev}: \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}$ as
\begin{equation}
    
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{ev}: (
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})) \times (
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}) \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}. \label{eq:mcg-canonical-action}
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The name $\infty$\textit{-mapping class group} in Definition~\ref{def:infty-mcg} refers to the fact that $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ is a generalization of the classical mapping class group (e.g. \cite{FarbMargalit2012}) of smooth manifolds. For $\mathcal{X} = X$ a compact smooth manifold, the $0$-truncation of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ recovers the mapping class group $\mathrm{MCG}(X)$ of $X$
    \begin{equation}
        \tau_{\leq 0}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) = \pi_0{\rm Diff}(X) = \mathrm{MCG}(X).
    \end{equation}
    Here $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ is the diffeological diffeomorphism group, whose $U$-points are smooth
    $U$-families of diffeomorphisms with smooth inverses. Since $\pi_0$ of the shape of a sheaf on
    $\mathrm{CartSp}$ is its set of concordance classes \cite[Example~4.3.50]{Sati_Schreiber_2026}, $\tau_{\leq 0}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ is the set of smooth isotopy classes
    of diffeomorphisms. For $X$ compact this agrees with $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(X)$ in the
    $C^\infty$ topology, since continuous isotopies can be smoothed. We use the convention
    $\mathrm{MCG}(X) = \pi_0\mathrm{Diff}(X)$ (no orientation constraint).
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
On an $\mathcal{X}$-valued $\sigma$-model, any electric symmetry \eqref{eq:electric-g-symmetry-homomorphism}
 \begin{equation}
     \rho: \mathsf{G} \to \flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}),
 \end{equation}
 and more generally any action
 \begin{equation}
     \hat{\rho}: \mathcal{G} \to \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})
 \end{equation}
 of a group object (Definition~\ref{app:def:gp-action}), acts on the magnetic charges.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-unit of $\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$
    \begin{equation}
        \eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_{\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}:\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \cong \mathbf{B}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})
    \end{equation}
    encodes a group object homomorphism $\Omega\eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_{\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}: \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$. The action of $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ on $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ is obtained by composing this group object homomorphism with the canonical action \eqref{eq:mcg-canonical-action} of Definition~\ref{def:infty-mcg}.

    For $\flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$, we also have a group object homomorphism induced by the points-to-pieces transform (Definition~\ref{app:def:pts-to-piec})
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{B}\flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})\cong  \flat \mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \xrightarrow{\epsilon_{\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}^{\flat}} \mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \xrightarrow{\eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_{\mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}} 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{B}\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \cong \mathbf{B}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}).
    \end{equation}
    Applying the internal hom functor $[\Sigma,-]$ yields the actions
    \begin{equation}
        \textbf{Sym}_e(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})\times \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}), \quad [\Sigma,\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})] \times \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}).
    \end{equation}
    These in turn induce the claimed actions by further composing with $[\Sigma,\rho]$ and $[\Sigma,\hat{\rho}]$, respectively.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:z2-electric}
We continue with $\mathcal{X} = S^1$ from Example~\ref{ex:magnetic-charges-s1}. Usually, $S^1$ is equipped with a metric $g$, so that the electric symmetries are classified by
\begin{equation}
   \flat  {\rm Isom}(S^1,g)\leq \flat {\rm Aut}(\mathcal{X}), \quad \flat{\rm Isom}(S^1,g) \cong \flat U(1) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2,
\end{equation}
and the magnetic charges are valued in $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^1 = \mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z}$.
The points-to-pieces transform is
\begin{equation}
    \flat U(1) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2 \to U(1) \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2 \to \mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z} \rtimes \mathbb{Z}_2.
\end{equation}
Thus, the action of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ on $\mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z}$ is the delooping 
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{B}r: \mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z}
\end{equation}
of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-automorphism of the integers
\begin{equation}
   r: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}, \quad r(1) = -1. 
\end{equation}
By contrast, $\flat U(1)$ acts trivially on the homotopy groups, but the induced action on $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^1$ is still nontrivial. The map $\mathbf B\flat U(1)\to \mathbf B\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbf B\mathbb{Z})$ is determined by $c_1$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
In \cite[Section 3.4]{Sheckler:2025rlk}, it is observed, for the case of $\mathcal{X} = X$ a smooth manifold, that the mapping class group $\mathrm{MCG}(X)$ acts on the lowest nontrivial homotopy group $\pi_k(X)$ of $X$ by combining the canonical action of $\mathrm{MCG}(X)$ on the \textit{homology} groups $H_{\bullet}(X)$ and the Hurewicz isomorphism $\pi_k(X) \to H_k(X)$. One would hope this action extends to all homotopy groups. However, ${\rm MCG}(X) = \tau_{\leq 0}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(X))$, so in general we only have the truncation morphism
\begin{equation}
    f: 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(X) \to {\rm MCG}(X),
\end{equation}
which cannot be used to induce a \textit{coherent} action of ${\rm MCG}(X)$ on $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X$, namely an action on the homotopy groups $\pi_k(X)$ compatible with their extension data, unless there exists a section for $f$. Thus, the precise statement is that $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(X)$ acts on $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X$, not simply $\mathrm{MCG}(X)$ by itself.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rmk:oka-principle}
    The reader should note that what we have constructed in this section are actions induced by the canonical evaluation action
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{ev}:\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{X}.
    \end{equation}
    This, however, should not be interpreted as saying that every action on the magnetic charges, which are in full generality described by group object homomorphisms $\mathcal{G} \to \mathrm{Aut}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X})$ valued in the automorphism group object of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$, is describable in this form. For this to be the case, a necessary condition is that
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:oka}
        
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 [\mathcal{X},\mathcal{X}] \overset{?}{\cong} [
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}],
    \end{equation}
    even before taking into account invertibility conditions. The equivalence \eqref{eq:oka} is called the \textit{smooth Oka principle}\footnote{We thank Urs Schreiber for bringing this to our attention.} \cite{Pavlov2014,BerwickEvans2024}, \cite[Theorem 4.3.54]{Sati_Schreiber_2026}, and can be shown to hold in general if one requires $\mathcal{X} = X$ to be a smooth manifold. It also underlies Proposition~\ref{prop:mch-shape-fields}. Dropping this condition allows one to construct counterexamples \cite[Section 5.2]{Sati_Schreiber_2026}.

    Even for $\mathcal{X}=X$ a smooth manifold, the sought statement
    \begin{equation}
        
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \overset{?}{\cong} \mathrm{Aut}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}),
    \end{equation}
    is not true in general. For instance, for $n\geq 5$ one has $\pi_0\mathrm{Diff}^+(S^n) \cong \Theta_{n+1}$,
    the group of homotopy $(n+1)$-spheres, e.g. $\mathbb{Z}_{28}$ for $n=6$, whereas every orientation-preserving
    self-homotopy equivalence of $S^n$ is homotopic to the identity \cite{kervaire-milnor1963,Cerf1970}.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
Given a choice of basepoint $\mathsf x: * \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$, one can define a co-action of magnetic charges on global electric symmetries
    \begin{equation}
    \text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}: \flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})\cong \flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times * \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}_{\flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}\times \mathsf x} \flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{pr}_{\flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})}, \alpha)} \flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X},
\end{equation}
where $\alpha$ is the action of $\flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ on $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$. In words, this corresponds to the orbits of $\mathsf x$ under $\flat \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$. One can similarly use the orbit of $\mathsf x$ to define a co-action on the full automorphism group
\begin{equation}
    \hat{\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}}: \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \to \mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X}) \times 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}.
\end{equation}
This co-action will not play an important role in this paper but we will explore it in future work concerning a unified treatment of electric and magnetic symmetries.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rmk:topological-families}
We emphasize that despite allowing for stackings with very general TFT's, we are still limiting the scope to topological theories, as opposed to considering dynamical metric-dependent general theories. This is a consequence of magnetic symmetries being constructed from the underlying topological charges. Sometimes, both kinds of stackings are considered side-by-side as ``families'' of QFT's (e.g. \cite{Cordova:2019jnf,Cordova:2019uob,McNamara:2020uza,Brennan:2026ira,Stockall:2025ngz}), where concepts familiar from symmetries such as mixed anomalies are considered. The reader will notice that a significant part of such discussions concerning general families of theories may be treated using the same methods used here, but the physical interpretation is different.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
In the pre-quantum field theory perspective \cite{nuiten2013cohomological} (cf. \cite[Section 5]{Schreiber:2013pra}), a cobordism $\Sigma: \Sigma_{\text{in}} \to \Sigma_{\text{out}}$ induces a span of field stacks
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pre-quantum-span}
    \mathbf{Fields}(\Sigma_{\text{in}},\mathcal{X}) \xleftarrow{\;(-)|_{\Sigma_{\text{in}}}\;} \mathbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \xrightarrow{\;(-)|_{\Sigma_{\text{out}}}\;} \mathbf{Fields}(\Sigma_{\text{out}},\mathcal{X}),
\end{equation}
and a phase-valued cocycle turns it into a pre-quantum correspondence. ``Motivic quantization'' is the expected linearization of such spans, rigorous at present for finite gauge theories (Dijkgraaf--Witten theory \cite{Freed1993,Freed:2009qp}). We use this picture only as motivation for the language of Section~\ref{ssec:dualization-against-tft}, where the dynamics of a theory is encoded by a map $\mathfrak D: \mathbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \mathcal D$ and magnetic symmetries act by stacking with the topological sector $[\Sigma,\mathcal{T}]$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:magnetic-backgrounds} Let $\Sigma \to \mathcal{X}$ be a $d$-dimensional $\sigma$-model. Let $\mathcal{T}\in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}$ be a \textit{choice} of \textit{dualizing object}, interpreted as a \textit{moduli stack of TFT's}, which we require to be
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item equipped with a reference object, $t: \mathcal{T}_0 \to \mathcal{T}$,
    \item $d$-truncated $\mathcal{T} \cong \tau_{\leq d} \mathcal{T}$.
\end{enumerate}
The higher stack of \textit{background fields} of the \textit{geometric magnetic $\mathcal{T}$-symmetries} is the mapping stack
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}):= [\Sigma,[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}],
\end{equation}
where $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0} \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}$ denotes the stack of $\mathcal{T}_0$-\textit{relative} maps, defined as the homotopy pullback
\begin{equation}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	{[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}} & {[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]} \\
	{\mathcal{T}_0} & {\mathcal{T}}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["{\mathrm{pr}_{\mathcal{T}_0}}"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{\mathrm{ev}_{\sf x}}", from=1-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow["t"', from=2-1, to=2-2]
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
of the reference object $t: \mathcal{T}_0 \to \mathcal{T}$ with the evaluation at $\mathsf{x}:* \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$.
We denote this stack by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-mag}
    \mathrm{Mag}_{(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)}(\mathcal{X},\mathsf x) := [
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0},
\end{equation}
and call it the \textit{stack for magnetic $\mathcal{T}$-symmetry backgrounds relative to $\mathcal{T}_0$} of $\mathcal{X}$,
so that $\mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})=[\Sigma,\mathrm{Mag}_{(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)}(\mathcal{X},\mathsf x)]$. When $\mathcal{T}_0=*$ and $t$
picks out the basepoint of $\mathcal{T}$, we shall write $\mathrm{Mag}_{\mathcal{T}}(\mathcal{X},\mathsf x):=[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{*}$, and
we omit $\mathsf x$ whenever the basepoint is clear from context.

A magnetic co-symmetry $\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}: 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to \mathsf{Y}$ determines geometric magnetic symmetry backgrounds via their image under the pullback
\begin{equation}\label{eq:induced-background-corho}
  [\Sigma,[\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}] : [\Sigma,[\mathsf{Y},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}] \to [\Sigma,[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}] = \mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}).
\end{equation}

More generally, we call a map of smooth stacks $s:\mathcal{S} \to \mathrm{Mag}_{(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)}(\mathcal{X})$ a
\textit{magnetic symmetry} of the $\sigma$-model, with $\mathcal S$ the target space for its
backgrounds, the case \eqref{eq:induced-background-corho} being that of $s$ factoring through
$[\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}:[\mathsf{Y},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}\to\mathrm{Mag}_{(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)}(\mathcal{X})$. The stack of
$\mathcal S$-background fields over $\Sigma$ is the mapping stack
$\left[\Sigma, \mathcal{S}\right] \to \mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma, \mathcal{X})$. We do not require $s$ to be
injective, so that $\mathcal S$ need not act effectively (Remark~\ref{rmk:non-effective}).
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
Let us unpack the preceding definitions in the following several remarks.
\begin{remarkparts}
\item  \label{rmk:t-is-flat-abstractly}
    Dualization is computed with respect to a smooth stack $\mathcal{T}$, so that the resulting TFT's are generally not flat, even though $\sf Y$ is discrete. For the differential-geometric target $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ and connected discrete $\mathsf Y$, however, the resulting TFT's are always flat (Remark~\ref{rmk:why-connections}).

    Notably, while, as summarized in Section~\ref{ssec:review-magnetic}, the abstract interpretation of cohomology operations valued in $\mathcal{T}$ draws from the higher pre-quantum field theory perspective of \cite{Schreiber:2013pra}, we do not impose the abelian group condition that the author of op. cit. requires on $\mathcal{T} = \textbf{Phases}$. Briefly, this is because in the context of generalized symmetries, we are interested in non-invertible and nonabelian symmetries, for which it is necessary to drop said condition. Our approach thus draws both from the pre-quantum perspective and from the bulk TFT's-as-spacetime-filling defects interpretation used in practice in the physics literature.

    That being said, the dualizing stack $\mathcal{T}$ is not a general stack either. The required conditions are physically motivated, as we now explain.
    
\item \label{rmk:t-is-pointed}
    We require $\mathcal{T}$ to have a reference object $t: \mathcal{T}_0 \to \mathcal{T}$ so that we have a notion of \textit{trivial} TFT: a TFT $f:\Sigma \to \mathcal{T}$ is trivial if it factors through $\mathcal{T}_0$
    \begin{equation}
        f \cong t\circ f_0: \Sigma \to \mathcal{T}_0 \to \mathcal{T}.
    \end{equation}
    The reference object also allows us to define relative maps. Working with general maps that are not relative introduces a factor of $\mathcal{T}$ in the mapping stack that, if not dealt with appropriately, introduces spurious degrees of freedom, as can be seen from dualizing $\mathsf{Y}=*$, which ought to encode trivial information
    \begin{equation}
        \text{unpointed:}\quad \left[ * , \mathcal{T} \right] \cong \mathcal{T}, \quad \text{relative:}\quad \left[*, \mathcal{T} \right]_{\mathcal{T}_0} \cong \mathcal{T}_0,
    \end{equation}
    the latter of which is physically irrelevant by hypothesis.

    More structurally, however, the canonical projection $\mathrm{pr}_{\mathcal{T}_0}:[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}\to \mathcal{T}_0$ built into the pullback square above distinguishes the passage to $\mathcal{T}_0$-relative maps as a way of \textit{reducing} $\mathcal{T}$-valued TFT data to $\mathcal{T}_0$-valued TFT data, and nothing in this reduction requires $\mathcal{T}_0$ to be a physically negligible theory: it could equally well be some other reference sector against which the magnetic $\mathcal{T}$-symmetry backgrounds are to be measured. Here, however, we do take $\mathcal{T}_0$ in the strict sense of a trivial TFT, so that the reduction to $\mathcal{T}_0$-relative maps has the effect of subtracting exactly the trivial contributions to the TFT, as above.

    In many cases, such as those involving theories on closed manifolds, it will be sufficient to consider $\mathcal{T}_0 = *$, so that $\mathcal{T}$ is more precisely a \textit{pointed} stack. In other cases, when boundary and edge modes need to be taken into account, other choices are required, but we will not cover these in the present work.
    
\item The $\mathcal{T}$-dualization computed by the mapping stack $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X},  \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ takes into account all possible (relative) morphisms without requiring any additional conditions. In other words, the target of magnetic symmetry backgrounds in great generality describes a \textbf{smooth $\infty$-groupoid of generalized relative nonabelian cohomology operations} \cite{Schreiber:2013pra,Fiorenza:2020dcp}.
    
    \item \label{rmk:-1-form-symmetry-background}
    The latter remark implies that the background magnetic symmetry fields considered in Definition~\ref{def:magnetic-backgrounds} are maps from $\Sigma$ to a smooth $\infty$-groupoid, which can be understood to encode a principal $\infty$-groupoid bundle. In other words, the magnetic backgrounds are \textit{generalized nonabelian cocycles}, much as in the case of electric symmetries \cite{Perez-Lona:2025xxm} covered in Section~\ref{ssec:review-electric}. As such, a single map
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:magnetic-symmetry-single-background}
        b: \Sigma \to \left[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X},  \mathcal{T}\right]_{\mathcal{T}_0}
    \end{equation}
    in $\mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ encodes, as in Equation~\eqref{eq:symmetry-map-p} for electric symmetries, a background for a \textit{tower} of magnetic symmetries whose form-degree runs one lower than the electric tower's, starting at the \textit{$(-1)$-form symmetries} (see below) rather than at ordinary $0$-form symmetries (Remark~\ref{rmk:variance-magnetic}(ii)). We can depict this schematically as follows:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:mag-symmetry-map-b}
    b: \left(  \begin{tikzcd}
\cdots \arrow[d, shift left] \arrow[d, shift left=3] \arrow[d, shift right] \arrow[d, shift right=3]          \\
{\coprod_{i,j,k \in {\cal I}} U_i\cap U_j\cap U_k} \arrow[d] \arrow[d, shift left=2] \arrow[d, shift right=2] \\
{\coprod_{i,j \in {\cal I}} U_i\cap U_j} \arrow[d, shift left] \arrow[d, shift right]                         \\
\coprod_{i \in {\cal I}} U_i                                                                                 
\end{tikzcd}\right) \to \left( \begin{tikzcd}
	\cdots \\
	{\{m:\eta'\circ\eta \Rrightarrow \eta''\}} \\
	{\{\eta:F \Rightarrow F'\}} \\
	{\{F: {
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}}\to \mathcal{T}\}}
	\arrow[shift left, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[shift left=3, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[shift right, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[shift right=3, from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=2-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow[shift left, from=3-1, to=4-1]
	\arrow[shift right, from=3-1, to=4-1]
\end{tikzcd}\right).
\end{equation}
    We remark that the assigned morphisms on the right are morphisms of sheaves. In contrast with electric symmetries, these assignments on the patches are generally \textit{smooth}, not necessarily locally constant. For $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ and connected $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$, however, these assignments are always locally constant, by the mechanism of Remark~\ref{rmk:why-connections}, hence on an equal footing with the electric case. Depending on the choices of $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)$, the magnetic symmetries may also encode connections themselves. These are \textit{refinements} beyond topological data that are often assumed in the physics literature for a heuristic (often, Lagrangian) interpretation in terms of locally defined differential forms.

    Physically, higher morphisms between morphisms are interpreted as non-genuine higher defects because they represent localized domain walls or interpolating interfaces that cannot exist in isolation, but must terminate on the boundaries of the genuine, standalone bulk cocycles they connect. In the Lagrangian framework, for example, these non-genuine defects and coboundary equivalences are exact (total derivative) terms added to the action, which integrate to zero on a closed, oriented bulk and thus yield negligible contributions to the path integral (the contributions stop being physically negligible to become observable localized edge modes if boundaries and higher corners are considered, but as previously stated we will not pursue this here).
    
    Part of the information in \eqref{eq:mag-symmetry-map-b} is given by functions on the patches
    \begin{equation}
        b_i: U_i \to \{F_i: 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to  \mathcal{T} \}
    \end{equation}
related by a $2$-cell defined on the intersections
\begin{equation}
    b_{ij}: U_{ij} \to \{\eta_{ij}:F_i \Rightarrow F_j\},
\end{equation}
which themselves, as already explained, are subject to higher coherence information. In particular, any global point of $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ defines a
\textit{constant} assignment on $\Sigma$
    \begin{equation}
        b: \Sigma \to \{F: 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to  \mathcal{T}\}.
    \end{equation}
    In other words, we obtain a \textbf{symmetry background field given by a parameter $b$} (constant, or smoothly varying, depending on $(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}_0)$), the hallmark of the so-called (magnetic) \textbf{$(-1)$-form symmetries.} These play an important role in much of the contemporary discussion of generalized symmetries.
    
\item \label{rmk:non-effective}
    The magnetic symmetries defined by the magnetic co-symmetry $\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}: 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \to \mathsf{Y}$ need not act effectively nor do they need to cover all magnetic symmetries proper to the $\sigma$-model, in the sense that the map of magnetic symmetries
    \begin{equation}
        [\Sigma, [\mathsf{Y}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}] \to \mathbf{Bgnd}_m(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})
    \end{equation}
    may have a nontrivial kernel relative to the trivial TFT's $\mathcal{T}_0$, namely $[\mathrm{cofib}(\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}),\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ (Example~\ref{ex:trivially-coacting-backgrounds}), and need not be surjective. This will be important when considering the \textit{gauging} of magnetic symmetries, which we address in the upcoming \cite{PerezLona:gauging}.
    
\item \label{rmk:t-d-truncated}
    The requirement of $\mathcal{T}$ being $d$-truncated (see Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncated}) characterizes an assumption that the topological defect TFT's $\Sigma \to \mathcal{T}$, as bulk theories, depend only on the homotopical data of $\Sigma$ up to degree $d$.
    
    For example, for $d\geq2$, $\pi_n(S^d)\neq0$ for infinitely many $n\geq d$. For a target smooth $\infty$-groupoid $\mathcal{X}$, the adjunction
    \begin{equation}
        \textbf{H}(S^d, \flat\mathcal{X}) = \textbf{H}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^d, \mathcal{X})
    \end{equation}
    shows that the $\mathcal{X}$-valued flat maps can probe the higher category-theoretic information of $\mathcal{X}$ beyond degree $d$. If $\mathcal{X}$ is $d$-truncated, however, then the maps factor through the $d$-truncation $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^d \to \tau_{\leq d}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^d$ (cf. Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncation}).

    The assumption, however, is at least partly based on the fact that the homotopy data of degree $d$, when passing to the \textit{stable} picture of (integral) homology, becomes generated by the spacetime fundamental cycle. That being said, it has been remarked that there is a relation between \textit{unstable} cohomology operations (which need not survive to homology) and \textit{non-invertible symmetries} \cite{Chen:2022cyw,Chen:2023czk,Pace:2023mdo}. Exploring geometric magnetic symmetries depending on homotopy groups of degree beyond that of spacetime dimension is an interesting open direction.
    \end{remarkparts}
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- remark-16: body_md -->
\label{rmk:variance-magnetic}
The assignment $\mathsf Y\mapsto[\mathsf Y,\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ is contravariant, so it reverses the variance of magnetic co-symmetries a second time.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \textit{Universal property.} A co-symmetry is a map \textit{out of} $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$, which is initial in $\textbf{H}_{\mathcal{X} /, \mathrm{disc}}$. A magnetic symmetry background induced by it, via \eqref{eq:induced-background-corho}, is a map \textit{into} $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$. It thus plays for magnetic symmetries the role that $\flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$, terminal among discrete actions (Remark~\ref{rmk:terminal-electric}), plays for electric symmetries.
\item \textit{Degree.} A $k$-form symmetry is parameterized locally by $k$-form data, but its background is a $(k+1)$-form: this shift by one, from symmetry to background, holds equally on the electric and magnetic sides, and is not what distinguishes them. What does distinguish them is which symmetry degree a given background tower starts at. $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ is the magnetic counterpart of the \textit{classifying} object $\mathbf{B}\flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ of electric backgrounds, not of the group $\flat\mathrm{Aut}(\mathcal{X})$ of electric transformations in \eqref{eq:symmetry-stack}. For instance, for $\mathcal{X}=S^1$, $\mathcal{T}=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ and $\mathcal{T}_0=*$, one has $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^1,\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*\cong\mathbf{B}^{d-1}\flat U(1)=\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{B}^{d-2}\flat U(1))$ (Example~\ref{ex:s1-target}), the background stack of a $(d-2)$-form $U(1)$ symmetry. Accordingly, the tower \eqref{eq:mag-symmetry-map-b} starts, in symmetry degree, at $-1$, one degree below the electric tower \eqref{eq:symmetry-map-p}, which starts at ordinary $0$-form symmetries (Remark~\ref{rmk:-1-form-symmetry-background}).
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-16 -->
<!-- remark-17: body_md -->
\label{rmk:local-systems}
A global point $a:
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{T}$ of $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]$ is a $\mathcal{T}$-valued $\infty$-local system on $\mathcal{X}$, that is, a flat $\infty$-connection \cite[Section 5.2.6]{Schreiber:2013pra}. By Proposition~\ref{prop:mch-shape-fields}, morphisms in $\mathbf{MCh}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ are \textit{large gauge transformations}. Since magnetic symmetry backgrounds act on magnetic charges through the evaluation of Remark~\ref{rmk:co-module-dualized-module}, they are $\mathcal{T}$-valued \textit{representations} of these large gauge transformations. For $\mathcal{T}=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$, these are higher one-dimensional representations. Transgressing over a closed $(d-1)$-dimensional slice $\Sigma_{d-1}$ turns them into rank-one $\infty$-local systems on $\mathbf{MCh}(\Sigma_{d-1},\mathcal{X})$ \cite[Section 5.4]{Fiorenza:2013jz}, which act on the topological quantum state spaces of \cite[Section 2.3.2]{Sati:2025vjw}.
<!-- end remark-17 -->
<!-- remark-18: body_md -->
\label{rmk:t-not-monoidal-gp} Notably, Definition~\ref{def:magnetic-backgrounds} \textit{does not require $\mathcal{T}$ to have a \textbf{composition law.}}\footnote{We thank Xingyang Yu for pointing out some of the references cited here.} While it is in practice often the case that $\mathcal{T}$ is a monoid object (and even a group object, as in the case of $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$, which will play a central role in this article), this requirement would automatically make $(-1)$-form symmetries composable. In the literature, it is frequently argued that $(-1)$-form symmetries circumvent the traditional requirement of a composition law, in that they are associated with \textit{sets} or \textit{spaces} of \textit{coupling constants} or \textit{parameters}, see for example \cite{Cordova:2019jnf,Cordova:2019uob,Heidenreich:2020pkc,McNamara:2020uza,Yu:2020twi,Vandermeulen:2022edk,Yu:2024jtk,Aloni:2024jpb,Rudelius:2024vmc,Robbins:2025apg}. 

Nevertheless, this should not be taken as meaning that composition laws of parameter spaces are altogether irrelevant. On the contrary, in specific applications of $(-1)$-form symmetries, and especially when related to gauging, composition laws are in fact necessary. We show in forthcoming work \cite{PerezLona:applications} that neglecting this additional structure yields gauged fields with spurious degrees of freedom. Indeed, already within the present article, our two main structural results, the fibration theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:descent-magnetic-symmetries}) and the factorization theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization}), require $\mathcal{T}$ to be not merely a monoid but a grouplike $E_\infty$-object (a condition $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ satisfies), since this is what identifies $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]$ with a connective spectrum and thereby grants access to the stable homotopy-theoretic tools these theorems rely on.
<!-- end remark-18 -->
<!-- remark-19: body_md -->
\label{rmk:t-d-module}
At this stage, it would seem natural to require $\mathcal{D}$ to be a $\mathcal{T}$-module (after $\Sigma$-fiber integration) $\triangleright: \mathcal{T} \times \mathcal{D} \to \mathcal{D}$, allowing the stacked theory to be compressed back into the original dynamical target space $\mathcal{D}$ as
\begin{equation}
   \Phi_m:  \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})\to  \mathcal{D}\times [\Sigma,\mathcal{T}] \xrightarrow{\triangleright\circ \left(\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal{D}} \times \int_{\Sigma}\right)} \mathcal{D}.
\end{equation}
This would return a theory described solely by its original kind of dynamics $\mathcal{D}$ (for example, as described below, for Lagrangian theories this is the tensoring operation of higher bundle gerbes with connection). While this is frequently the case, we do not impose this $\mathcal{T}$-module condition generically (Remark~\ref{rmk:t-not-monoidal-gp}).
<!-- end remark-19 -->
<!-- remark-20: body_md -->
\label{rmk:co-module-dualized-module}
The crucial implication of dualizing magnetic co-symmetries is that it turns a co-module structure into a module structure, \textit{up to bulk TFT's}. This is the concrete form of the double reversal of variance: electric symmetries act on $\mathcal{X}$, magnetic co-symmetries co-act on $\mathcal{X}$, and magnetic symmetries act on $\mathbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$ up to bulk TFT's.

The $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$-co-module structure on $\mathcal{X}$
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{X} \xrightarrow{\Delta_{\mathcal{X}}} \mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{X} \xrightarrow{\eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_{\mathcal{X}} \times {\rm id}_{\mathcal{X}}} \left(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \right) \times \mathcal{X},
\end{equation}
induces a co-module structure on $\textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X})$
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \times \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}).
\end{equation}
By Proposition~\ref{prop:mch-shape-fields}, this is the field stack co-acted on by its own shape. The evaluation map
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \times \textbf{Bgnd}_{m}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \to \left[\Sigma, \mathcal{T}\right]
\end{equation}
yields a module structure up to bulk TFT's
\begin{equation}
   \textbf{Bgnd}_{m}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \times \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \textbf{Bgnd}_{m}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \times  \textbf{MCh}(\Sigma, \mathcal{X}) \times \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}) \to \left[\Sigma, \mathcal{T} \right] \times \textbf{Fields}(\Sigma,\mathcal{X}).
\end{equation}
This is reminiscent of the well-known algebraic result that if $M$ is a $C$-co-module, with coaction $\delta_M: M\to C\otimes_{\textbf{k}} M$, for $C$ a coalgebra over a field $\textbf{k}$, then $M$ is a $C^{\vee}$-module for $C^{\vee}:={\rm Hom}(C,\textbf{k})$, the dual algebra \cite[Chapter II]{sweedler1969hopf} 
\begin{equation}
    C^{\vee}\otimes_{\textbf{k}} M \xrightarrow{{\rm id}_{C^{\vee}}\otimes \delta_M} C^{\vee} \otimes_{\textbf{k}} C \otimes_{\textbf{k}} M \xrightarrow{{\rm ev} \otimes {\rm id}_M} \textbf{k} \otimes_{\textbf{k}} M \xrightarrow{\cong} M,
\end{equation}
and may be understood as its unstable geometric shadow. We comment on this in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.
<!-- end remark-20 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:trivially-coacting-backgrounds}
Let $q\circ\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}:
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}\to\mathsf C=\mathrm{cofib}(\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}})$ be the associated trivially-co-acting magnetic co-symmetry of Definition~\ref{def:trivially-acting-magnetic-co-symmetry}. Since $q\circ\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}$ factors through the terminal object $*$ up to homotopy, the induced magnetic symmetry backgrounds factor as
\begin{equation}
    [q\circ\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}: [\mathsf{C}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0} \to [*, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0} \cong \mathcal{T}_0 \to [
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}, \mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}.
\end{equation}
Thus, as expected, the induced magnetic symmetries act only via $\mathcal{T}_0$ theories. In particular, for $\mathcal{T}_0 = *$ there are no induced theories whatsoever.

In fact, more is true. Since $[-,\mathcal{T}]$ sends homotopy pushouts to homotopy pullbacks, the cofiber square of Definition~\ref{def:trivially-acting-magnetic-co-symmetry} gives
\begin{equation}
    [\mathsf C,\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}\ \cong\ [\mathsf Y,\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}\times_{[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}}\mathcal{T}_0,
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{T}_0\to[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ is the inclusion of the trivial backgrounds. For $\mathcal{T}_0=*$, this is the fiber sequence
\begin{equation}
    [\mathsf C,\mathcal{T}]_*\longrightarrow[\mathsf Y,\mathcal{T}]_*\xrightarrow{[\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}},\mathcal{T}]_*}[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_*.
\end{equation}
In words, $[\mathsf C,\mathcal{T}]_{\mathcal{T}_0}$ is the \textit{kernel}, relative to the trivial theories $\mathcal{T}_0$, of the map of magnetic symmetry backgrounds induced by $\text{\scalebox{-1}[1]{$\rho$}}$. This means that the backgrounds for the $\mathsf C$-symmetry \textit{act trivially} on the $\sigma$-model, characterized universally. Hence, the cokernel of a co-symmetry dualizes to the kernel of the corresponding magnetic symmetry, exactly as the double reversal of variance (Remark~\ref{rmk:variance-magnetic}) predicts. This will play a crucial role in our discussion of gauging of magnetic symmetries in \cite{PerezLona:gauging}.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- remark-21: body_md -->
\label{rmk:why-connections}
On a closed, oriented $d$-manifold $\Sigma$, maps of stacks compute \textit{sheaf} cohomology, $\pi_0[\Sigma,\mathbf B^dU(1)]\cong H^d(\Sigma,\underline{U(1)})$ \cite[Proposition 3.2.20]{FSS12}. By the exponential sequence \eqref{eq:exp} and Lemma~\ref{lem:soft} (Section~\ref{sec:higher-pontryagin-symmetries}), this is $H^{d+1}(\Sigma,\mathbb{Z})$, which agrees with singular cohomology since $\Sigma$ is locally contractible, and hence vanishes for dimensional reasons. This means that bundle $(d-1)$-gerbes without connection carry no phase weights on closed $\Sigma$, so that if working with $\mathbf B^dU(1)$ as target, flatness would have to be imposed \textit{by hand}. With $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$, by contrast, \textit{weights are instead holonomies}, and dualizing the discrete charges $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$ against it yields the flat backgrounds as a natural consequence, as expected on physical grounds (Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization}, also Remark~\ref{rmk:flatness-from-connections}). In brief, working with smooth stacks with connections, \textit{the flatness of magnetic symmetry backgrounds is not imposed but derived}.
<!-- end remark-21 -->
<!-- remark-22: body_md -->
\label{rmk:fiber-cofiber}
The Postnikov tower encodes distinguished \textit{fiber sequences}: each stage $\mathsf{X}_{n+1}$ sits in a fibration, where $X:=\vert
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}\vert$
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{B}^{n+1}\pi_{n+1}(X) \to \mathsf{X}_{n+1} \to \mathsf{X}_n. \label{eq:postnikov-fiber-sequences}
\end{equation}
More generally, as used in \cite{Sheckler:2025rlk}, we have a sequence of fibrations of magnetic charges
\begin{center}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	&& {\mathbf{B}^d \pi_d(X)} && {\mathbf{B}^{n+2}\pi_{n+2}(X)} & {\mathbf{B}^{n+1}\pi_{n+1}(X)} & \\
	{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}} & \cdots & {\mathsf{X}_{d}\cong \tau_{\leq d}
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}} & \cdots & {\mathsf{X}_{n+2}} & {\mathsf{X}_{n+1}} & {\mathsf{X}_n}
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=1-5, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=1-6, to=2-6]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=2-3]
	\arrow[from=2-3, to=2-4]
	\arrow[from=2-4, to=2-5]
	\arrow[from=2-5, to=2-6]
	\arrow[from=2-6, to=2-7]
\end{tikzcd},
\end{center}
which dualizes to the sequence of magnetic symmetry backgrounds
\begin{center}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	& {[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X},\mathcal{T}]_*} \\
	& \cdots \\
	{[\mathbf{B}^d \pi_d(X),\mathcal{T}]_*} & {[\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*} \\
	& \cdots \\
	{[\mathbf{B}^{n+2}\pi_{n+2}(X),\mathcal{T}]_*} & {[\mathsf{X}_{n+2},\mathcal{T}]_*} \\
	{[\mathbf{B}^{n+1}\pi_{n+1}(X),\mathcal{T}]_*} & {[\mathsf{X}_{n+1},\mathcal{T}]_*} \\
	& {[\mathsf{X}_n,\mathcal{T}]_*}
	\arrow[from=2-2, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=2-2]
	\arrow[from=3-2, to=3-1]
	\arrow[from=4-2, to=3-2]
	\arrow[from=5-2, to=4-2]
	\arrow[from=5-2, to=5-1]
	\arrow[from=6-2, to=5-2]
	\arrow[from=6-2, to=6-1]
	\arrow[from=7-2, to=6-2]
\end{tikzcd}.
\end{center}
Notice, however, that $[-,\mathcal{T}]_*$ sends \textit{cofiber} sequences, and not fiber sequences, to fiber sequences. The Postnikov fiber sequences \eqref{eq:postnikov-fiber-sequences} are therefore not preserved. In a stable setting, fiber and cofiber sequences coincide. We discuss this further in Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}.
<!-- end remark-22 -->
<!-- remark-23: body_md -->
\label{rmk:postnikov-backgrounds}
    While Remark~\ref{rmk:fiber-cofiber} shows that we cannot merely transfer all the fiber sequences of the Postnikov tower of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ to sequences of magnetic symmetries, we can nevertheless use the Postnikov decomposition of the mapping stack $[\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*$ itself. This yields the fibrations
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{B}^k \pi_k\left([\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*\right) \to \tau_{\leq k}\left([\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*\right) \to \tau_{\leq k-1}\left([\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*\right),
    \end{equation}
    and importantly a fiber inclusion
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{B}^{d-1} \pi_{d-1}\left([\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*\right) \to [\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_* \to \tau_{\leq d-2}\left([\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*\right),
    \end{equation}
    into the genuine stack for magnetic symmetry backgrounds. This uses that $[\mathsf{X}_d,\mathcal{T}]_*$ is $(d-1)$-truncated, and is in a sense an alternative reconstruction process to the cofiber approach above.
<!-- end remark-23 -->
<!-- remark-24: body_md -->
\label{rmk:physics-first-postnikov}
    A physics interpretation of the magnetic symmetries \eqref{eq:first-postnikov-mag-map} comes from observing that $\mathbf{B}^n \pi_n(X)$ is the target space for pure $\mathbf{B}^{n-1} \pi_n(X)$ higher discrete gauge theory. Given the equivalence $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathbf{B}^{n} \pi_n(X) \cong \mathbf{B}^{n} \pi_n(X)$, the mapping stack $[\mathbf{B}^{n} \pi_n(X), \mathcal{T}]_*$ already classifies its magnetic symmetries.
    
    Hence, universally, $\mathcal{X}$-valued $\sigma$-models receive, via
\eqref{eq:first-postnikov-mag-map}, the magnetic symmetries of
$\mathbf{B}^{n-1}\pi_n(X)$ gauge theory. This map, importantly, need \textit{not} be injective
(Remark~\ref{rmk:non-effective}). For instance, for $\mathcal{T}=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ with $d\geq3$ and
$\mathcal{X}=\mathbf B_\nabla\mathrm{Pin}^-(2)$, whose first nontrivial Postnikov stage is
$\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2$, the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ in homotopy degree $d-3$ of $[\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathcal{T}]_*$ does not survive
(Section~\ref{sssec:pin2}).
<!-- end remark-24 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:descent-magnetic-symmetries}
Let $\mathcal H$ be a group object of $\textbf{H}$ acting on a pointed object $(\mathcal{X},x)$, and let

 \mathcal H.

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a grouplike $E_\infty$-object of $\textbf{H}$, not necessarily $d$-truncated. Then:

(\mathcal{X}

{\mathcal H}) \cong (
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X})
  \IfBooleanTF{#1}
    {\big/\mkern-7mu\big/}

\mathsf H

  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
(\mathcal{X}

{\mathcal H}),\mathcal{T}] \cong [

\mathcal{X}$.
