<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:pontryagin-factorization}
Let $X\in\mathrm{ob}\,\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ be pointed and connected, let
$d\geq1$, and write
\begin{equation}
    H_n:=H_n(X,\mathbb Z),\qquad \widehat{H_n}:=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(H_n,U(1))
\end{equation}
for the integral homology groups of $X$ and their Pontryagin duals as \textit{abstract} abelian groups. Then there is a non-canonical equivalence of abelian
$\infty$-group stacks
\begin{equation}\label{eq:box1}
    \left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*
    \;\cong\;
    \prod_{n=1}^{d}
    \mathbf{B}^{d-n}\mathrm{Dsc}\left(\widehat{H_n}\right).
\end{equation}

In particular, the mapping stack
$\left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*$ lies in the essential image of the
discrete inclusion
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Dsc}:\infty\mathrm{Grpd}\longrightarrow\textbf{H}.
\end{equation}
As always in this article, ``discrete'' is meant in the cohesive sense, and so in particular the mapping stack
need \textit{not} be $0$-truncated. Its homotopy sheaves are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pontryagin-homotopy-sheaves}
    \pi_k\left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*
    \cong
    \widehat{H_{d-k}}
    \cong
    H^{d-k}(X,U(1)),
    \qquad 0\leq k\leq d-1,
\end{equation}
and vanish otherwise.

In differential-cohomological terms, every background classified by
$\left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*$ has vanishing curvature. Thus the
higher Pontryagin magnetic symmetry backgrounds are flat as
differential cocycles.

If, in addition, every $H_n$ for $1\leq n\leq d$ is finitely
generated, so that we can write
\begin{equation}
    H_n\cong\mathbb Z^{r_n}\oplus T_n,
\end{equation}
where $T_n$ is finite, then we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:box2}
    \left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*
    \;\cong\;
    \prod_{n=1}^{d}
    \mathbf{B}^{d-n}
    \left(
        (\flat U(1))^{r_n}
        \times
        \mathrm{Dsc}(\widehat{T_n})
    \right).
\end{equation}

The equivalences above depend on a choice of splitting of the reduced
integral chain complex of $X$ into two-term free resolutions of its
homology groups and, for \eqref{eq:box2}, additionally on choices of
splittings $H_n\cong\mathbb Z^{r_n}\oplus T_n$. They are therefore not
natural in $X$ in general. The homotopy sheaves
\eqref{eq:pontryagin-homotopy-sheaves} are canonical and natural in $X$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:cotensor}
		For $X\in\mathrm{ob\,}\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ and $\mathcal Y\in\mathrm{ob}\,\textbf{H}$, there is an equivalence
		$[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y]\cong\lim_{X}\mathcal Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, \textbf{H}$. In particular, for every
		$U\in\mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$, we have that
		\begin{equation}
		\left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y\right](U)\ \cong\ \mathrm{Map}\left(X,\ \mathcal Y(U)\right),
        \end{equation}
        where $\mathrm{Map}\left(X,\ \mathcal Y(U)\right) \in \mathrm{ob}\, \infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ is the internal hom in $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The functor $\mathrm{Dsc}$ preserves colimits and the terminal object, so using $X\cong\operatorname*{colim}_{X}\ast$ in $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$, we get $\mathrm{Dsc}(X)\cong\operatorname*{colim}_{X}\ast$ in $\textbf{H}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:mapping-colimit}, we have
    $[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y]\cong\lim_{X}[\ast,\mathcal Y]\cong\lim_{X}\mathcal Y$.
    Limits in $\textbf{H}\subseteq\mathrm{PSh}_\infty(\mathrm{CartSp})$ are computed sectionwise, and the limit of the constant diagram at $\mathcal Y(U)$ over $X$ is the cotensor $\mathcal Y(U)^X=\mathrm{Map}(X,\mathcal Y(U))$, so the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:cotensor-pointed}
    Let $X\in\mathrm{ob}\,\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$ be pointed by $x:\ast\to X$, and let $\mathcal Y\in\mathrm{ob}\,\textbf{H}$ be pointed. Then for every $U\in\mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$,
    \begin{equation}
        [\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y]_{*,\mathrm{Dsc}(x)}(U)\ \cong\ \mathrm{Map}_*\left(X,\mathcal Y(U)\right).
    \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By definition, $[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y]_{*,\mathrm{Dsc}(x)}=\mathrm{fib}\left(\mathrm{ev}_{\mathrm{Dsc}(x)}:[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal Y]\to\mathcal Y\right)$, the fiber over the basepoint of $\mathcal Y$. Fibers in $\textbf{H}$ are computed sectionwise, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:cotensor}, $\mathrm{ev}_{\mathrm{Dsc}(x)}(U)$ is the evaluation $\mathrm{Map}(X,\mathcal Y(U))\to\mathcal Y(U)$ at $x$, meaning precomposition with $x$. The fiber over the basepoint is $\mathrm{Map}_*(X,\mathcal Y(U))$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:split}
		There is an isomorphism of chain complexes of abelian groups
		\begin{equation}
		\widetilde C_\bullet\ \cong\ \bigoplus_{n\ge1}R^{(n)},\quad
		R^{(n)}=\left[\,B_n\hookrightarrow Z_n\,\right],
        \end{equation}
		where each $R^{(n)}$, concentrated in degrees $n+1,n$, is a length-one free resolution of $H_n=H_n(X,\mathbb{Z})$ placed in
		degree $n$ (as familiar from the proof of the universal coefficient theorem, e.g. \cite[Section~3.1]{hatcher2002algebraic}).
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Subgroups of free abelian groups are free abelian in any rank, so $Z_n$ and
		$B_{n-1}$ are free. The latter gives that the following exact sequences always split
		\begin{equation}
        0\to Z_n\to\widetilde C_n\xrightarrow{\partial}B_{n-1}\to0.
        \end{equation}
        If we now \textit{choose} splittings
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:hc-splitting}
		    \widetilde C_n\cong Z_n\oplus B_{n-1},
		\end{equation}
         the map $\partial$ annihilates the summand
		$Z_n$ and carries the summand $B_{n-1}\subseteq\widetilde C_n$ onto
		$B_{n-1}\subseteq Z_{n-1}\subseteq \widetilde C_{n-1}$. Regrouping gives the claimed direct sum decomposition.
        
        Finally, note that each $R^{(n)}$ has $H_{n+1}=\ker(B_n\hookrightarrow Z_n)=0$ and
		$H_n=Z_n/B_n=H_n(X,\mathbb{Z})$, with both terms free. The sum starts at $n=1$ because
		$\widetilde C_0=0$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- remark-29: body_md -->
The fact that the splitting of the theorem we are aiming to prove is not natural in $X$ stems exactly from having made a choice of splitting \eqref{eq:hc-splitting}.
<!-- end remark-29 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:factor}
		Let $\mathcal P\cong\prod_{i\in I}\mathcal P_i$ be a product of presheaves of
		pointed spaces, with the product and projections preserving the chosen
		basepoints. If $\mathcal P$ satisfies descent, then every $\mathcal P_i$
		satisfies descent.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Using the basepoints in all factors other than $i$, the presheaf $\mathcal P_i$
		is a retract of $\mathcal P$:
        \begin{equation}
            \mathcal P_i \xrightarrow{\imath_{i}} \prod_{j\in I}\mathcal P_j \xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_i}\mathcal P_i.
        \end{equation}
        Since the full subcategory of presheaves satisfying
		descent is closed under retracts, $\mathcal P_i$ satisfies descent.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:dk-splitting}
Let $X$ be pointed and connected in $\infty\mathrm{Grpd}$, and $\mathcal F$ an abelian $\infty$-group stack in $\textbf{H}$. More explicitly, $\mathcal F$ is taken to be a sheaf on $\mathrm{CartSp}$
valued in connective $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules, presented objectwise by a connective complex of
sheaves of abelian groups $C$, so that 
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{F}(U)\;\cong\;\mathrm{DK}\left(C(U)\right)
\end{equation}
naturally in $U \in \mathrm{ob\,CartSp}$. (Here ``sheaf'' means that descent holds homotopically, not as a strict limit in $\mathrm{sAb}$.)

Let $H_n:=H_n(X,\mathbb{Z})$ and 
$R^{(n)}=\left(B_n\hookrightarrow Z_n\right)$, concentrated in degrees $n+1,n$, be the
free resolution of $H_n[n]$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:split}. Then there is an
equivalence of abelian $\infty$-group stacks
\begin{equation}\label{eq:dk-splitting}
  \left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal{F}\right]_*
  \;\cong\;
  \prod_{n\ge1}\mathcal{P}^{(n)},
  \quad
  \mathcal{P}^{(n)}:=\mathrm{DK}\left(\tau_{\ge0}\,\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}\left(R^{(n)},C\right)\right),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{P}^{(n)}$ is obtained from the objectwise
complexes $U\mapsto\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}\left(R^{(n)},C(U)\right)$, which compute
$U\mapsto\mathbf{R}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}\left(H_n,C(U)[-n]\right)$. For every $U\in\mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$ and $k\geq0$, the homotopy presheaf of
$\mathcal P^{(n)}$ fits objectwise into the universal coefficient
sequence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ucseq}
\begin{split}
0\longrightarrow&
\mathrm{Ext}^1_{\mathbb Z}\left(
    H_n,H_{k+n+1}\left(C(U)\right)
\right)
\longrightarrow
\pi_k\left(\mathcal P^{(n)}(U)\right)
\\
\longrightarrow&
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\left(
    H_n,H_{k+n}\left(C(U)\right)
\right)
\longrightarrow0 .
\end{split}
\end{equation}
These sequences are natural in $U$ and hence assemble into an exact
sequence of presheaves. They split non-canonically after evaluation at
each $U$, but need not split as a sequence of presheaves or sheaves.
The homotopy sheaves of $\mathcal P^{(n)}$ are obtained by sheafifying
the corresponding homotopy presheaves.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Let $U\in \mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$ be a probing space. By Corollary~\ref{cor:cotensor-pointed} and the hypothesis, we get that
\begin{equation}
  \left[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathcal{F}\right]_*(U)
  \;\cong\;\mathrm{Map}_*\left(X,\mathrm{DK}(C(U))\right)
\end{equation}
naturally in $U$. For any connective complex of abelian groups $D$,
adjunction between the reduced normalized chain complex and Dold--Kan gives an equivalence of simplicial abelian groups natural in $D$:
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{Map}_*\left(X,\mathrm{DK}(D)\right)
  \;\cong\;
  \mathrm{DK}\left(\tau_{\ge0}\,\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}\left(\widetilde{C}_\bullet(X,\mathbb{Z}),D\right)\right).
\end{equation}
This is \eqref{eq:DK}
with $D=M[d]$ replaced by a general connective $D$, the proof being unchanged.
Since $\widetilde{C}_\bullet$ is levelwise free, $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}
(\widetilde{C}_\bullet,D)$ moreover computes
$\mathbf R\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(\widetilde{C}_\bullet,D)$, which is used below. Here
$\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\widetilde{C}_\bullet,D)_k=\prod_j\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(\widetilde{C}_j,D_{j+k})$.

Applying this with $D=C(U)$ and inserting the decomposition
$\widetilde{C}_\bullet\cong\bigoplus_{n\ge1}R^{(n)}$ of
Lemma~\ref{lem:split} yields \eqref{eq:dk-splitting} objectwise. This follows from the facts that $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(-,C(U))$ carries direct
sums to products, and that $\tau_{\ge0}$ commutes with products because products of abelian groups are exact. The splitting of
$\widetilde{C}_\bullet$ is chosen once and for all, before any coefficient object appears, and
in particular is independent of $U$. Thus, $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(-,C)$ applied to it is natural in the coefficient sheaf and the decomposition is an equivalence of presheaves of pointed spaces. The left-hand side satisfies descent, being an internal hom into a stack, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:factor} \textit{each factor} does as well. Now, \eqref{eq:dk-splitting} is a natural weak equivalence of presheaves between two stacks, so it is an equivalence of stacks. But since all the maps above are additive, this is in fact an equivalence of stacks of connective $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules.

Finally, $R^{(n)}$ is a bounded complex of free abelian groups resolving
$H_n[n]$. Therefore, for every $U\in\mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$,
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\left(R^{(n)},C(U)\right)
    \cong
    \mathbf R\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\left(H_n[n],C(U)\right)
    \cong
    \mathbf R\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\left(H_n,C(U)[-n]\right).
\end{equation}
Since $R^{(n)}$ is a length-one free resolution, its homology is
described by the objectwise universal coefficient sequence
\eqref{eq:ucseq}. Good truncation preserves homology in nonnegative
degrees. These objectwise sequences are moreover natural in $U$, so they form
an exact sequence of presheaves, and the corresponding homotopy sheaves
are their sheafifications.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:soft}
    The sheaves $\underline{\mathbb{R}}=C^\infty(-,\mathbb{R})$ and $\Omega^j$, $j\geq1$, are modules over the sheaf of rings $C^\infty$, which admits smooth partitions of unity. They are therefore fine, hence soft. In particular, they are acyclic: $H^{k}(Y,\underline{\mathbb{R}})=0$ and $H^{k}(Y,\Omega^j)=0$ for all $k\ge1$ and all paracompact smooth manifolds $Y$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lem:deligne}
    Let $d\geq1$, and let
    \begin{equation}
        A_d\ :=\ \left[\ \underline{\mathbb{Z}}\ \hookrightarrow\ C^\infty(-,\mathbb R)\ \xrightarrow{\ d\ }\ \Omega^1\ \to\ \cdots\ \to\ \Omega^d\ \right],
    \end{equation}
    reindexed as a connective chain complex $C$ of sheaves on $\mathrm{CartSp}$, with the sheaf $\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ in degree $d+1$, $C^\infty(-,\mathbb R)$ in degree $d$, and $\Omega^j$ in degree $d-j$ for $1\le j\le d$, so that for any probing space $U\in\mathrm{ob}\,\mathrm{CartSp}$ we have that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)(U)\ \cong\ \mathrm{DK}\left(C(U)\right).
    \end{equation}
    The objectwise Dold--Kan presheaf $U\mapsto\mathrm{DK}(C(U))$ already satisfies descent on $\mathrm{CartSp}$ (for \v{C}ech covers, and also for hypercovers by the same argument), so it agrees with its stackification.
In particular, for every $U$, its objectwise homotopy
groups are the ordinary homology groups of the complex $C(U)$,
\begin{equation}
    \pi_k\left(\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)(U)\right)
    \cong H_k\left(C(U)\right),
\end{equation}
and these are
\begin{align}
    H_{d+1}\left(C(U)\right)&=0,\\
    H_d\left(C(U)\right)&\cong U(1),\\
    H_j\left(C(U)\right)&=0,
      \qquad 0<j<d,\\
    H_0\left(C(U)\right)
      &=
      \Omega^d(U)/d\Omega^{d-1}(U).
\end{align}
The first three lines already define sheaves on $\mathrm{CartSp}$, so that, in
positive degrees, the homotopy sheaves are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deligne-positive-homotopy-sheaves}
    \pi_d(\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1))\cong\mathrm{Dsc}(U(1)),
    \qquad
    \pi_j(\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1))=0
    \quad (0<j<d).
\end{equation}
In degree zero,
\begin{equation}
    \pi_0(\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1))\cong\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
We first show that the objectwise Dold--Kan presheaf $U\mapsto\mathrm{DK}(C(U))$
already satisfies descent on $\mathrm{CartSp}$. Covering families in $\mathrm{CartSp}$ may be
taken to be differentiably good open covers, whose nonempty finite
intersections are again Cartesian spaces. Each term of $C$ is acyclic on every
Cartesian space: $C^\infty(-,\mathbb R)$ and the $\Omega^j$ are fine, hence soft,
modules over $C^\infty$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:soft}), and $\underline{\mathbb{Z}}$ is constant with
$H^k(U,\underline{\mathbb{Z}})=0$ for $k\geq1$ since $U$ is contractible. Since $C$ is bounded,
the \v{C}ech hypercohomology of $C$ on any such cover is computed by the
complex of sections, so the objectwise presheaf satisfies (hyper)descent, and
its values on $\mathrm{CartSp}$ agree with those of $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$
\cite[Section 3.2.3]{FSS12}.

We now compute the homology of $C(U)$. The injectivity of
$\underline{\mathbb{Z}}(U)\hookrightarrowC^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ gives
$H_{d+1}(C(U))=0$. Since $U$ is connected,
$
    \ker\left(d:C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)\to\Omega^1(U)\right)
    =\mathbb R,
$
so
$
    H_d(C(U))\cong\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\cong U(1).
$
For $0<j<d$, the relevant portion of $C(U)$ is exact by the
Poincar\'e lemma, hence $H_j(C(U))=0$. Finally,
$
    H_0(C(U))=\Omega^d(U)/d\Omega^{d-1}(U).
$

The first three homology groups already define sheaves on $\mathrm{CartSp}$,
giving \eqref{eq:deligne-positive-homotopy-sheaves}. In degree zero, the
map induced by the exterior derivative,
\[
    \Omega^d(U)/d\Omega^{d-1}(U)
    \xrightarrow{\;\cong\;}
    \Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}(U),
    \qquad
    [\omega]\longmapsto d\omega,
\]
is injective because every closed $d$-form on the contractible space
$U$ is exact, and it is surjective because every closed $(d+1)$-form
on $U$ is exact. This identifies $H_0(C(U))$ with $\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}(U)$
naturally in $U$, giving $\pi_0(\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1))\cong\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}$.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-30: body_md -->
\label{rmk:flatness-from-connections}
    Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne} is where flatness enters. A pointed map out of the discrete, connected stack $\mathrm{Dsc}(X)$ into $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ only sees the higher gauge transformations of the trivial bundle $(d-1)$-gerbe with zero connection (cf.\ Proposition~\ref{app:prop:counits}), and such gauge transformations are necessarily flat. Indeed, at level $k$ for $1\leq k\leq d$, they are
classified by $\Omega^k\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\cong\flat\mathbf B^{d-k}U(1)$. In particular, at the top level these are constant $U(1)$-valued functions. We are thus constructing higher gerbes with connection out of the discrete magnetic charges $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$, and the only connection data these can carry are flat.
<!-- end remark-30 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne}, Proposition~\ref{prop:dk-splitting} applies with $\mathcal F=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ and $C$ the reindexed additive Deligne complex. The only nonzero homology groups of $C(U)$ are $H_0(C(U))$ and $H_d(C(U))\cong U(1)$, the latter independent of $U$. Since $n\geq1$ and $k\geq0$, $H_0(C(U))$ never enters \eqref{eq:ucseq}. The term $\mathrm{Ext}^1_\mathbb{Z}(H_n,U(1))$ vanishes because $U(1)$ is divisible, hence an injective $\mathbb{Z}$-module. Therefore the connective complex of presheaves
\begin{equation}
    K^{(n)}:=\tau_{\geq0}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}\left(R^{(n)},C\right),\qquad \mathcal P^{(n)}=\mathrm{DK}\left(K^{(n)}\right),
\end{equation}
is acyclic for $n>d$, so that $\mathcal P^{(n)}\cong*$. For $1\leq n\leq d$, it has a single nonzero homology presheaf, the constant presheaf $\widehat{H_n}$ in degree $d-n$. The good truncations then give a zigzag of objectwise quasi-isomorphisms, natural in $U$,
\begin{equation}
    K^{(n)}\xleftarrow{\ \cong\ }\tau_{\geq d-n}K^{(n)}\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }\widehat{H_n}[d-n].
\end{equation}
Applying Dold--Kan, we obtain objectwise equivalences
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal P^{(n)}\cong\mathrm{DK}\left(\widehat{H_n}[d-n]\right)\cong\mathbf B^{d-n}\mathrm{Dsc}\left(\widehat{H_n}\right)
\end{equation}
between presheaves satisfying descent, hence an equivalence of abelian $\infty$-group stacks. Taking the product over $1\leq n\leq d$ proves \eqref{eq:box1}. The homotopy sheaves follow, with $\widehat{H_m}\cong H^m(X,U(1))$ by the universal coefficient theorem and the injectivity of $U(1)$.

Since both $\mathrm{Dsc}(X)$ and $[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*$ are discrete, the evaluation map $\mathrm{Dsc}(X)\times[\mathrm{Dsc}(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*\to\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ has discrete source, and hence factors through the counit $\epsilon_{\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)}^{\flat}:\flat\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\to\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ (Proposition~\ref{app:prop:counits}). But the composition of this counit with the curvature map $\flat\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\to\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1) \to \Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}$ is trivial, thus establishing that backgrounds always have vanishing curvature.

Finally, if $H_n\cong\mathbb Z^{r_n}\oplus T_n$, then $\widehat{H_n}\cong U(1)^{r_n}\times\widehat{T_n}$ as abstract abelian groups, and $\mathrm{Dsc}(U(1))\cong\flat U(1)$. This proves \eqref{eq:box2}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- remark-31: body_md -->
\label{rmk:scope-pontryagin}
The choice $\mathcal{T}=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ detects the invertible symmetries given by flat $U(1)$-cohomology of the target. These coincide with the bosonic invertible solitonic symmetries of \cite[Proposition 4.10]{Chen:2023czk}, which need not exhaust all bosonic invertible symmetries \cite[Section 4.3.2]{Chen:2023czk}. Nor does $\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$ see symmetries generated by invertible spin theories. For the $4$d $\mathbb{CP}^1$ model, the invertible part of the hopfion symmetry is $\mathbb{Z}_2$, generated by a spin bordism invariant \cite{Chen:2022cyw}. Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization} with $X=S^2$ and $d=4$ instead gives $[
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 S^2,\mathbf{B}^{4}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*\cong\mathbf{B}^2\flat U(1)$, with no hopfion factor, while the bosonic parts agree. Capturing such symmetries requires a different dualizing object $\mathcal{T}$ (Section~\ref{sec:conclusion}).
<!-- end remark-31 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:BG}
    Let $\mathsf G=\mathrm{Dsc}(G_0)$ be a discrete $\infty$-group, and let $d\ge1$. Then
    \begin{equation}
        \left[\mathbf{B}\mathsf G,\ \mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*\ \cong\ \prod_{n=1}^{d}\mathbf{B}^{\,d-n}\,\mathrm{Dsc}\left(\widehat{H_n(BG_0,\mathbb{Z})}\right),
        \qquad \pi_k\cong\widehat{H_{d-k}(BG_0,\mathbb{Z})}\quad (0\le k\le d-1).
    \end{equation}
    In particular, $\pi_{d-1}\cong\widehat{\pi_0(G_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}}$. If $G_0$ is furthermore $0$-truncated, the $H_n(BG_0,\mathbb{Z})$ are the integral group homology groups $H_n(G_0,\mathbb{Z})$ with trivial action on the coefficients, and $\pi_{d-1}\cong\widehat{G_0^{\mathrm{ab}}}$, the Pontryagin dual of the abelianization of $G_0$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization} to $X=BG_0$, and use $H_1(BG_0,\mathbb{Z})\cong\pi_1(BG_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}=\pi_0(G_0)^{\mathrm{ab}}$ by the Hurewicz theorem.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
For $G_0$ a \textit{finite} group, all $H_n(G_0,\mathbb{Z})$ with $n\ge1$ are finite, and by the
    universal coefficient theorem
    $\widehat{H_n(G_0,\mathbb{Z})}\cong H^{n}(G_0,U(1))\cong H^{n+1}(G_0,\mathbb{Z})$ for $n\ge1$. Hence
    \begin{equation}
        \left[\mathbf{B}\mathsf G,\ \mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)\right]_*\ \cong\ \mathrm{Dsc}\left(\prod_{n=1}^{d}B^{\,d-n}H^{n}(G_0,U(1))\right) \cong\ \prod_{n=1}^{d}\mathbf{B}^{d-n}\mathrm{Dsc}\left(H^{n}(G_0,U(1))\right),
    \end{equation}
    a \textit{discrete} stack with no continuous moduli. These are the higher Pontryagin magnetic symmetries of finite gauge theory, e.g. Dijkgraaf--Witten theory in $d$ dimensions.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- remark-32: body_md -->
\label{rmk:BG-group-cohomology}
    At the level of connected components, $\pi_0[\mathbf{B}\mathsf G,\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*\cong H^d(BG_0,U(1))$ is the (higher) group cohomology of $G_0$ with coefficients in $U(1)$ with its discrete topology. Evaluated at the point, the elements of $[\mathbf{B}\mathsf G,\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*$ are thus $U(1)$-valued group $d$-cocycles, along with their (higher) coboundaries. These form the flat part of differential cohomology (e.g. \cite{CheegerSimons1985,hopkins2005quadratic}).\footnote{Another place in the context of symmetries where cohomology groups of discrete groups coming from continuous groups are discussed is \cite{Jia:2025vrj,Jia:2025uun}, where the authors investigate a possible classification of 't Hooft topological anomalies of Lie groups. The discrete groups have however a different origin. There, \textit{very schematically}, the computation corresponds to classes of maps $[\flat G, \mathbf{B}^dU(1)]$.}
<!-- end remark-32 -->
<!-- remark-33: body_md -->
\label{rmk:BG-postnikov}
The physical interpretation of Corollary~\ref{cor:BG} becomes clearer if we specialize to the first nontrivial Postnikov stage of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X}$ which, as discussed in Section~\ref{ssec:postnikov-towers}, is always of the form $\mathbf{B}^k \pi_k(X)$ for $X:=\vert 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} \vert$ and some $k\geq 1$. There are two notable kinds of symmetries in this case:
        \begin{enumerate}
    \item A constant map $\Sigma\to[\mathbf B^k\pi_k(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*$ at $\omega$. Evaluated at the point, $\omega$ is a $U(1)$-valued $d$-cocycle on $\mathbf B^k\pi_k(X)$, equivalently a group $d$-cocycle of the $(k-1)$-group $\mathbf B^{k-1}\pi_k(X)$. The cocycle is globally defined on $\Sigma$.

    Briefly specializing further to $k=1$, in terms of \v{C}ech data, the evaluation map pairs a \v{C}ech 1-cocycle $\{g_{ij} \in \pi_1(X)\}$ representing magnetic charge with the cocycle $\omega\in Z^d(\pi_1(X),U(1))$ representing the cohomology class, the same on every patch since the map is constant (and in any case locally constant by Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization}), yielding on $(d+1)$-fold overlaps $U_{i_0 \dots i_d}$ a $U(1)$-valued \v{C}ech $d$-cocycle given by evaluating the local group cocycle on the transition elements as
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:-1-form-discrete-torsion}
    c_{i_0 \dots i_d} = \omega(g_{i_0 i_1}, g_{i_1 i_2}, \dots, g_{i_{d-1} i_d}).
    \end{equation}
    
    Depending on the context and dimension, these are called \textit{discrete torsion} \cite{Vafa:1986wx, Sharpe:1999pv, Sharpe:1999xw, Sharpe:2000ki, Brunner:2014lua}, or \textit{(constant) theta angle term}\footnote{In the physics literature, this is often understood as the Chern--Weil representative of the instanton term, which requires differential form fluxes. That picture is, however, already assuming differential lifts of topological information. Here, by contrast, we are proceeding systematically, and will encounter expressions in terms of differential forms only after explicitly lifting from the strictly discrete to the generally cohesive realm. This will be covered in the upcoming \cite{PerezLona:gauging}.} \cite{Aharony:2013hda, Kapustin2014, Gaiotto:2014kfa}. Since these are background fields for symmetries, we understand a \textit{choice} of a globally defined $d$-cocycle as the background field of a $(-1)$-form symmetry, which couples the $\sigma$-model to a $d$-dimensional \textit{Dijkgraaf--Witten TFT} for $\pi_1(X)$ \cite{Dijkgraaf1990, Freed1993, Wakui1992} (and their higher generalizations for higher $k$, e.g. \cite{Yetter:1993dh,Porter:1996tz,doi:10.1142/S0218216597000145,Fiorenza:2013jz,Monnier:2015qxa}). A gauge transformation of this background field amounts to a shift by a coboundary, which contributes trivially on a closed, oriented $\Sigma$, showing that at this level of analysis, it is only the cohomology class of $\omega$ that is physical.
    
    \item On the other end, we have the factor $\mathbf{B}^{d-k}\mathrm{Dsc}\left(\widehat{\pi_k(X)}\right) \to [\mathbf{B}^k\pi_k(X),\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*$, where $\widehat{\pi_k(X)}\cong H^1_{\rm gp}(\pi_k(X),U(1))$. We can recognize this to be the magnetic symmetry backgrounds for a $(d-k-1)$-form $\widehat{\pi_k(X)}$ symmetry, the \textbf{\textit{Pontryagin dual magnetic symmetry.}} Again, in terms of \v{C}ech data on a good open cover $\{U_i\}$ of $\Sigma$, the evaluation map as a cohomology operation is the \v{C}ech cup product that pairs a $k$-cocycle $\{g_{i_0 \dots i_k} \in \pi_k(X)\}$ representing the magnetic charge as a \textit{flat} higher principal $\mathbf{B}^{k-1}\pi_k(X)$-bundle with a $(d-k)$-cocycle $\{\chi_{i_0 \dots i_{d-k}} \in \widehat{\pi_k(X)}\}$, necessarily locally constant, representing the higher dual background field. On $(d+1)$-fold overlaps $U_{i_0 i_1 \dots i_d}$, this yields a $U(1)$-valued $d$-cocycle defined as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:topological-pontryagin-cocycle}
\omega_{i_0 \dots i_d} = \chi_{i_k \dots i_d}(g_{i_0 \dots i_k}) \in Z^d(\Sigma, U(1))
\end{equation}
whose integration over $\Sigma$ is the $U(1)$ phase of the coupled topological theory.
\end{enumerate}
The magnetic symmetries of other degrees correspond to the cohomology groups $H^m(K(\pi_k(X),k),U(1))$, encompassing a wide array of cohomology operations.
<!-- end remark-33 -->
<!-- remark-34: body_md -->
The cohomology groups of Eilenberg--MacLane spaces were studied in the influential papers \cite{HochschildSerre1953,Serre1953,EilenbergMacLane1953,EilenbergMacLane1954,SHC_1954-1955__7_1_A11_0}. These cohomology groups are in general quite involved, often requiring more specialized computational techniques (see e.g. \cite{Clement2002Integral}), so we will limit ourselves to a few highlights. 

First of all, we remark that the naive expectation concerning the relation between $H^d_{\rm sing}(B^nK,A)$ and $H^{d-n+1}_{\rm sing}(BK,A)\cong H^{d-n+1}_{\rm gp}(K,A)$ does not hold
\begin{equation}
    H^d_{\rm sing}(B^nK,A) \not\cong H^{d-n+1}_{\rm sing}(BK,A)\cong H_{\rm gp}^{d-n+1}(K,A).
\end{equation}
Instead, these groups are related via the canonical map $\Sigma B^nK \to B^{n+1}K$ inducing the suspension homomorphism (e.g. \cite{hatcher2002algebraic})
\begin{equation}
    \sigma^*: H^{q+1}_{\rm sing}(B^{n+1}K,A)\to H^{q+1}_{\rm sing}(\Sigma B^n K,A) \cong H^q_{\rm sing}(B^n K, A),
\end{equation}
which is an isomorphism for $q< 2n$ and a monomorphism for $q=2n$, but otherwise need not be injective or surjective. In particular, for the cohomology group of degree $k$, we let $q=n+k$, and we obtain an isomorphism when $k<n$.

This means that for sufficiently large $n$, the cohomology groups \textit{stabilize} into stable cohomology groups $H^k_{\rm stable}(K,A)$.

An exceptional case, used in Remark~\ref{rmk:BG-postnikov}, is that of $H^d_{\rm sing}(B^dK,A)$, where we do obtain a genuine isomorphism with group cohomology groups
\begin{equation}
    H^d_{\rm sing}(B^dK,A) \cong H^1_{\rm sing}(BK,A) \cong H^1_{\rm gp}(K,A).
\end{equation}

Notably, these computations are highly nontrivial almost exclusively due to the \textit{torsional} part. If one works with rational coefficients, for example, then the computations simplify significantly (e.g. \cite{Serre1953}, \cite[Section 19]{EilenbergMacLane1954}). Since we are nevertheless presently interested in $U(1)$-valued Lagrangians, and not in $\mathbb{Q}$-valued TFT's, we will not pursue this route here.
<!-- end remark-34 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{ex:s1-target}
    For $\mathcal{X} = S^1$ the smooth circle, which serves as the target space for e.g. the \textit{two-dimensional compact boson}, we have $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 \mathcal{X} = \mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z} = \mathrm{Dsc}(B\mathbb{Z})$. Therefore, $H_1=\mathbb{Z}$ and $H_{n\ge2}=0$, giving
	\begin{equation}
    [\mathbf{B}\mathbb{Z},\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)]_*\cong\mathbf{B}^{d-1}\flat U(1).
    \end{equation}
    This classifies the magnetic symmetry backgrounds for the so-called \textit{winding} $U(1)$ \textit{symmetry}. We study this in greater detail in forthcoming work \cite{PerezLona:applications}.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- remark-35: body_md -->
\label{rmk:torsion-deloopings}
    The torsion factors $\mathbf{B}^{d-n}\widehat{H_n}$ appearing above, such as $\mathbf{B}^{j}\mathrm{Dsc}(\mathbb{Z}_2)$ and $\mathbf{B}^{j}\mathrm{Dsc}(\mathbb{Z}_6)$, arise only for $k\geq2$, the homology of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathcal{X}$ being torsion-free for $k=0,1$. Both the free and torsion factors are discrete. The distinction is that the free factors are copies of the divisible group $\flat U(1)$, whose continuous structure, the associated currents, only becomes visible once the charges are differentially refined (as we shall do explicitly in \cite{PerezLona:gauging}), while the torsion factors have no such structure to begin with. One might expect the torsion factors to descend from the free ones through the inclusions $\mathbb{Z}_p\hookrightarrow U(1)$, which induce maps $\mathbf{B}^{j}\mathbb{Z}_p\to\mathbf{B}^{j}\flat U(1)$. This is not what happens, since the torsion factors sit in degrees $n$ distinct from those of the free factors. This means that for $k\geq2$ the stack of pointed maps out of $\mathbf{B}^{k+1}\mathbb{Z}$ is genuinely not a product of deloopings of $\flat U(1)$ alone, as soon as $d\geq k+3$.
<!-- end remark-35 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
Fix $d\geq3$ throughout (we return to $d=2$ in Remark~\ref{pin:remd2}), and take the
dualizing stack to be $\mathcal{T}=\mathbf{B}^{d}_{\nabla}U(1)$, $\mathcal{T}_0=*$, as in the rest of this section. Let
$G_\pm=\mathrm{Pin}^\pm(2)$ \cite{Kirby_Taylor_1991} for the two double covers, sitting in the extension
\begin{equation}
1\to U(1)\to G_\pm\xrightarrow{D}\mathbb{Z}_2\to1.
\end{equation}
Conjugation by any
lift $e\in D^{-1}(1)$ of the nontrivial element acts on $U(1)=\mathrm{Spin}(2)$ by inversion, so that for
$z\in U(1)$,
\begin{equation}\label{pin:conjugation}
(ez)^2=eze z=e^2(e^{-1}ze)z=e^2z^{-1}z=e^2.
\end{equation}
Every element of the non-identity component therefore squares to the same element $e^2=\pm1$, which can be checked to be central.
 It is precisely this sign that distinguishes the two groups: for $\mathrm{Pin}^+$ one has $e^2=1$, and the
subgroup $\langle e\rangle$ splits the extension, giving $G_+\cong U(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2\cong O(2)$, whereas for
$\mathrm{Pin}^-$ every element of the non-identity component instead has order $4$, so that no such splitting
exists and $G_-\cong\mathrm{Pin}(2)=U(1)\sqcup jU(1)\subset SU(2)$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{pin:BPin2}
$\dim_{\mathbb F_2}H^n(BG_-,\mathbb F_2)=1$ for $n\equiv0,1,2\pmod4$ and vanishes for
$n\equiv3\pmod4$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
This result is known, see e.g. \cite[Section 2.1]{Manolescu:2013bha}.
Since $G_-\cong\mathrm{Pin}(2)=N_{SU(2)}(U(1))$ is the normalizer of a maximal torus, $SU(2)/G_-=(SU(2)/U(1))/\mathbb{Z}_2=S^2/\{\pm1\}\cong\mathbb{RP}^2$,
with the residual Weyl group acting freely by the antipodal map. This exhibits $BG_-$ as the
total space of a fibration $\mathbb{RP}^2\to BG_-\to BSU(2)\cong\mathbb{HP}^\infty$. The
base is simply connected with $H^*(\mathbb{HP}^\infty,\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[v]$, $|v|=4$, so the $E_2$
page $E_2^{p,q}=\mathbb F_2[v]\otimes H^*(\mathbb{RP}^2,\mathbb F_2)$ of the associated Serre spectral
sequence is concentrated in $p\equiv0\pmod4$ and $0\leq q\leq2$. Any differential
$d_r\colon E_r^{p,q}\to E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}$ between two nonzero groups would need $r\equiv0\pmod4$ and
$q\geq r-1\geq3$, which is impossible given $q\leq2$. Hence, the spectral sequence collapses at $E_2$,
and this gives the stated dimensions.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{pin:beta}
We have that $\beta_+=0$ and $\beta_-\neq0$. Equivalently, the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on $\mathbf B^2\mathbb{Z}$ underlying~\eqref{pin:fib}
admits a homotopy fixed point for $\mathrm{Pin}^+(2)$, and none for $\mathrm{Pin}^-(2)$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
By obstruction theory (see e.g.\ \cite[Section~4.3]{hatcher2002algebraic}), a fibration over $B\mathbb{Z}_2$ with fiber $K(\mathbb{Z}^-,2)$ admits a section exactly
when its $k$-invariant vanishes, and a section of $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
(\mathcal{X}
  \IfBooleanTF{#1}
    {\big/\mkern-7mu\big/}
    {/\mkern-6mu/}
\mathcal{H})\to\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2$ is the same datum as
a homotopy fixed point, as follows from the proofs of Lemmas~\ref{lem:equivariant-pointed}
and~\ref{lem:equivariant-point}. For $G_+$, the group-theoretic splitting exhibited above directly gives
a section of $\mathbf BG_+\to\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2$, so $\beta_+=0$. For $G_-$, let
$u\in H^1(B\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb F_2)$ denote the generator. Then $u^3\neq0$, while
$p^*u^3\in H^3(BG_-,\mathbb F_2)=0$ by Lemma~\ref{pin:BPin2}. If we had a section $s$, naturality
would force $u^3=s^*p^*u^3=0$, which is a contradiction. Therefore, no such section exists and $\beta_-\neq0$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{pin:route1}
For both signs, $\pi_{d-1}\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}(\mathbf BG_\pm)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$. Moreover,
$\pi_{d-2}\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}(\mathbf BG_\pm)\cong\ker(d_2)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_2$ and
$\pi_{d-3}\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}(\mathbf BG_\pm)\cong\mathrm{coker}(d_2)$. In other words, the entire difference between the two signs,
which is confined to stems $d-2$ and $d-3$, is due to this single differential~\eqref{pin:eqd2}.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
We can apply Corollary~\ref{cor:nonnegative-abutment}, since the
relevant stems are nonnegative for $d\geq3$, together with the
non-equivariant splitting
\begin{equation}
    [
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
(\mathcal{X}
  \IfBooleanTF{#1}
    {\big/\mkern-7mu\big/}
    {/\mkern-6mu/}
\mathcal H),\mathcal{T}]
    \cong
    \mathcal{T}\oplus\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{X}
  \IfBooleanTF{#1}
    {\big/\mkern-7mu\big/}
    {/\mkern-6mu/}
\mathcal H)
\end{equation}
induced by evaluation at the chosen basepoint
(Corollary~\ref{cor:red-pointed}).

By Lemma~\ref{lem:deligne}, the only nonzero homotopy sheaves of $\mathcal{T}$
are
\begin{equation}
    \pi_d\mathcal{T}\cong\mathrm{Dsc}(U(1)),
    \qquad
    \pi_0\mathcal{T}\cong\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^{d+1}.
\end{equation}
The degree-zero sheaf meets the stems under consideration only when
$d=3$, in stem $d-3=0$, through the entry $E_1^{0,0}=\Omega_{\mathrm{cl}}^4$. This entry is in the image of the spectral sequence for
$\mathcal{T}^{h\mathbb{Z}_2}$ under the equivariant constant-map inclusion
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{const}:\mathcal{T}\longrightarrow M.
\end{equation}
By naturality, it consists of permanent cycles. Moreover, no
differential can hit it because it lies in filtration $s=0$. But this is
exactly the contribution of the constant $\mathcal{T}$-summand that is removed when
passing from the unpointed mapping stack to $\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}$. Therefore, it
does not affect the calculation of
$\pi_{d-3}\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}(\mathbf BG_\pm)$. The remaining entries in stems $d-1$, $d-2$, and $d-3$ are those above. The only possibly nonzero differential among them is
\eqref{pin:eqd2}, so the kernel and cokernel claims follow.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{pin:transgression}
Let $A=U(1)$, with its discrete topology, and let $f_-\colon\mathbb{Z}^-\to A^+$,
$a\mapsto(-1)^a$, which generates
$\pi_{d-2}Q\cong H^0(\mathbb{Z}_2,U(1)^-)\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}_2}(\mathbb{Z}^-,A^+)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$
(see~\eqref{pin:Q-answer}). Then the connecting map
$\partial\colon\pi_{d-2}Q\to\pi_{d-3}[\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathcal{T}]_*\cong H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$
satisfies $\partial(f_-)=(f_-)_*(\beta_\pm)$. In particular, $\partial=0$ for
$\mathrm{Pin}^+(2)$, and $\partial$ is an isomorphism for $\mathrm{Pin}^-(2)$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $E=
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
\mathbf BG_\pm$ and $B=\mathbf B\mathbb{Z}_2$. For $Y$ pointed and connected,
the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:pontryagin-factorization} identifies
$\pi_{d-n}[Y,\mathcal{T}]_*\cong\widetilde H^n(Y,A)$ for $1\leq n\leq d$. This identification
is natural in $Y$: it comes from~\eqref{eq:DK}, before any splitting is chosen. The
first map of the fiber sequence of Lemma~\ref{lem:pointed-fiber} is precomposition
with $p$, so on $\pi_{d-n}$ it is $p^*\colon H^n(B,A)\to H^n(E,A)$. Exactness of the
associated long exact sequence at $\pi_{d-3}[B,\mathcal{T}]_*$ ($d\geq3$) then gives
\begin{equation}
  \mathrm{im}(\partial)=\ker\left(p^*\colon H^3(B,A)\to H^3(E,A)\right).
\end{equation}

For $\mathrm{Pin}^+(2)$, the section $s$ of $p$ from Lemma~\ref{pin:beta} gives
$s^*p^*=\mathrm{id}$, so $p^*$ is injective and $\partial=0=(f_-)_*(\beta_+)$.

For $\mathrm{Pin}^-(2)$, recall that $\beta_-\in H^3(B,\mathbb{Z}^-)$ is, by definition, the class of
the section $k$ of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-twisted Eilenberg--MacLane fibration over $B$ with fiber
$K(\mathbb{Z}^-,3)$ that classifies~\eqref{pin:fib}, so that $E$ is the homotopy pullback of
the zero section along $k$. Hence $k\circ p$ is homotopic over $B$ to the zero
section, i.e.\ $p^*\beta_-=0$ in $H^3(E,p^*\mathbb{Z}^-)$. Naturality of the change of
coefficients along the equivariant map $f_-$ gives
$p^*\left((f_-)_*\beta_-\right)=(f_-)_*(p^*\beta_-)=0$, so
$(f_-)_*\beta_-\in\mathrm{im}(\partial)$. By Lemmas~\ref{pin:beta}
and~\ref{pin:fminus}, $(f_-)_*\beta_-$ generates $H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$. Hence
$\partial\colon\mathbb{Z}_2\to\mathbb{Z}_2$ is surjective, thus an isomorphism, and
$\partial(f_-)=(f_-)_*(\beta_-)$.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-36: body_md -->
\label{pin:transgression-rmk}
Lemma~\ref{pin:transgression} can be read as the familiar statement that the
fundamental class of the fiber $K(\mathbb{Z},2)$ transgresses to the Postnikov invariant
$\beta_\pm$. The proof above uses only exactness and naturality, and does not rely
on identifying $\partial$ with a differential of the Serre spectral sequence.
<!-- end remark-36 -->
<!-- remark-37: body_md -->
\label{pin:remd2}
For $d=2$, the stem $d-3=-1$ falls outside the connective range, and the argument above must be adapted
using the stable homotopy fixed points of Lemma~\ref{lem:stable-connective-hfp}. There, $\pi_0\mathrm{Mag}_\mathcal{T}$ is
the kernel of the analogous stable connecting map to $\pi_{-1}=H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,U(1))$, while the conclusions for
the stems $d-1,d-2$ are unchanged.
<!-- end remark-37 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{pin:transfer}
$H_n(BG_\pm,\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12])\cong H_n(BU(1),\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12])_{\mathbb{Z}_2}$, the coinvariants under
$c\mapsto-c$, which for $n\leq4$ evaluate to $0,0,0,\mathbb{Z}[\tfrac12]$ for $n=1,2,3,4$. It follows that
$H_n(BG_\pm,\mathbb{Z})$ is a finite $2$-group for $1\leq n\leq3$, while $H_4$ has rank $1$ and no odd
torsion.
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
This is the usual transfer argument for finite coverings (e.g.\ \cite[Section~3.G]{hatcher2002algebraic}). The map $BU(1)\to BG_\pm$ is a $2$-sheeted covering, and the composite of transfer
followed by projection is multiplication by $2$, so that after inverting $2$ the homology of
$BG_\pm$ is identified with the image of the projection map, namely the coinvariants of the
deck involution, which acts on $H_{2j}(BU(1))$ by $(-1)^j$. Finiteness away from this rational
part holds because $BG$ is of finite type for any compact Lie group $G$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{pin:Hminus}
$H_1=\mathbb{Z}_2$, $H_2=0$, $H_3=0$, $H_4=\mathbb{Z}$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{pin:BPin2}, the mod-$2$ Betti numbers are $1,1,1,0,1$ in degrees $0,\dots,4$. In degree
$2$, $1=\dim(H_2\otimes\mathbb F_2)+1$ forces $H_2\otimes\mathbb F_2=0$, hence $H_2=0$ by
Lemma~\ref{pin:transfer}. In degree $3$, $0=\dim(H_3\otimes\mathbb F_2)$ gives $H_3=0$ directly. In
degree $4$, $1=\dim(H_4\otimes\mathbb F_2)+0$. Writing $H_4=\mathbb{Z}\oplus T$ with $T$ a finite $2$-group by
Lemma~\ref{pin:transfer}, the vanishing $T\otimes\mathbb F_2=0$ forces $T=0$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{pin:Hplus}
$H_1=\mathbb{Z}_2$, $H_2=\mathbb{Z}_2$, $H_3=\mathbb{Z}_2$, $H_4=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Here $H^*(BO(2),\mathbb F_2)=\mathbb F_2[w_1,w_2]$ \cite[Theorem 7.1]{MilnorStasheff}, with Betti numbers $1,1,2,2,3$
in degrees $0,\dots,4$. The Wu formula \cite[Problem 8-A]{MilnorStasheff} gives $\mathrm{Sq}^1w_2=w_1w_2+w_3=w_1w_2$ and
$\mathrm{Sq}^1w_1=w_1^2$, so that the mod-$2$ Bockstein acts on bases as $w_1\mapsto w_1^2$ in degree
$1$, $w_1^2\mapsto0$ and $w_2\mapsto w_1w_2$ in degree $2$, $w_1^3\mapsto w_1^4$ and $w_1w_2\mapsto0$ in degree
$3$, and $w_1^4\mapsto0$, $w_1^2w_2\mapsto w_1^3w_2$ and $w_2^2\mapsto0$ in degree $4$. The resulting $E_2$
page of the Bockstein spectral sequence therefore vanishes in degrees $1,2,3$ and equals
$\mathbb F_2\langle w_2^2\rangle$ in degree $4$. Since $E_2^n$ simultaneously detects
$\mathrm{rank}\,H^n(-,\mathbb{Z})$ and the $\mathbb{Z}/2^{k\geq2}$ summands of $H^n(-,\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{n+1}(-,\mathbb{Z})$, and since
$\mathrm{rank}\,H^4=1$, there are no such higher-order summands in $H_n$ for $n\leq4$. Counting
dimensions then gives, in degree $2$, $2=\dim(H_2\otimes\mathbb F_2)+1$, so $H_2=\mathbb{Z}_2$. In degree $3$,
$2=\dim(H_3\otimes\mathbb F_2)+1$, so $H_3=\mathbb{Z}_2$. In degree $4$, $3=\dim(H_4\otimes\mathbb F_2)+1$,
so $H_4=\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}_2$, of rank $1$ and with no odd torsion by Lemma~\ref{pin:transfer}, in agreement with the known integral cohomology of $BO(n)$ \cite[Theorem 1.6]{Brown:1982BO} \cite[Theorem 2]{Feshbach:1983BO}.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{app:eq:internal-external}

The \textit{external hom} is a bifunctor
\begin{equation}
   \textbf{H}\left(-,-\right): \textbf{H}^{\rm op}\times \textbf{H} \to \infty{\rm Grpd}
\end{equation}
which, for $X,Y \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}$, computes the \textit{bare} $\infty$-groupoid of maps
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{H}(X,Y) \in \infty\rm Grpd.
\end{equation}

The \textit{internal hom} is a bifunctor
\begin{equation}
    \left[-,-\right]: \textbf{H}^{\rm op} \times \textbf{H} \to \textbf{H},
\end{equation}
which, for $X,Y \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}$, computes the \textit{smooth} $\infty$-groupoid of maps
\begin{equation}
    \left[X,Y\right] \in \rm ob\, \textbf{H},
\end{equation}
which is again an object in \textbf{H}. It establishes that $\textbf{H}$ is Cartesian closed in that
\begin{equation}
    \left[X \times Y, Z\right] \cong \left[X, \left[Y, Z \right]\right].
\end{equation}

The internal and external hom-objects are related by evaluating the sheaf $\left[X,Y\right] \in \rm ob \, \textbf{H}$ at the point $*\in \rm ob\, CartSp$ \cite[Observation 5.2.1]{Schreiber:2013pra}:
\begin{equation}
    \left[X,Y\right](*) \cong \textbf{H}\left(X,Y\right),
\end{equation}
and more generally for a probing space $U \in {\rm ob\, CartSp}$
\begin{equation}
    \left[X,Y\right](U) \cong \textbf{H}\left(U \times X, Y\right).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{app:def:terminal-co-slice}

For $A \in {\rm ob}\,\textbf{H}$, the \textit{slice topos} $\textbf{H}_{/A}$ is the category whose objects are morphisms $\left(f:B \to A \right) \in 1{\rm Mor}\,\textbf{H}$. Its $1$-morphisms are commutative diagrams
\begin{equation}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	B && {B'} \\
	& A
	\arrow["g", from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "f"', from=1-1, to=2-2]
	\arrow["{f'}", from=1-3, to=2-2]
	\arrow["\eta", Rightarrow, from=1-3, to=0]
\end{tikzcd},
\end{equation}
and higher morphisms are similar higher commutative diagrams.

Analogously, the co-slice category $\textbf{H}_{A/}$ is the category whose objects are morphisms $\left(f:A \to B \right) \in 1{\rm Mor}\,\textbf{H}$. Its $1$-morphisms are commutative diagrams
\begin{equation}
\begin{tikzcd}
	& A & \\
	\\
	B && {B'}
	\arrow["f"', from=1-2, to=3-1]
	\arrow[""{name=0, anchor=center, inner sep=0}, "{f'}", from=1-2, to=3-3]
	\arrow["g"', from=3-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow["\eta", Rightarrow, from=3-1, to=0]
\end{tikzcd},
\end{equation}
and so on.

The slice $\textbf{H}_{/A}$ is again an $\infty$-topos, with its own internal and external homs. The co-slice $\textbf{H}_{A/}$, by contrast, is not an $\infty$-topos in general.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{app:ex:pointed-slice}
    For $A=*$ the terminal object, the slice topos is $\textbf{H}$ itself
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{H}_{/*} \cong \textbf{H}.
\end{equation}
Moreover, the co-slice
\begin{equation}
    \textbf{H}_{*/} \cong \textbf{H}_{\rm ptd}
\end{equation}
is the $\infty$-category of \textit{pointed} smooth $\infty$-groupoids, whose objects are pairs $\left( A \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}, f:* \to A\right)$. It is closed symmetric monoidal with respect to the smash product $\wedge$.

In particular, the internal hom of $(\textbf{H}_{*/},\wedge)$ is the stack of \textit{pointed maps} $[X,Y]_* \in {\rm ob}\,\textbf{H}_{*/}$, namely maps $f:X \to Y$ which preserve the basepoints, $f(x)\cong y$, pointed by the constant map.

The stacks of unpointed maps $[X,Y]$ and pointed maps $[X,Y]_*$ are related by the evaluation map at the basepoint of $X$:
	\begin{equation}
		\mathrm{ev}_{x} \colon [X, Y] \to Y \quad \text{where} \quad f \mapsto f(x).
	\end{equation}
The pointed mapping stack is equivalent to the homotopy fiber of this evaluation map over the basepoint $y: *\to Y$:
	\begin{equation}
			[X,Y]_* \cong {\rm hofib}\left(\mathrm{ev}_{x} \colon [X, Y] \to Y \right).
            \end{equation}
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
The \textit{simplex category} $\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ has the finite ordinal numbers $[n] = \{0,1,\dots,n\}$ as objects, and weakly monotone functions $f\colon [n]\to[m]$ as morphisms
    \begin{equation}
        0\le i\le j\le n \Rightarrow f(i)\le f(j).
    \end{equation}
   We have morphisms
   \begin{enumerate}
       \item $\delta^n_i: [n] \to [n+1]$ for $i\in [n+1]$. The morphism includes $[n]$ into $[n+1]$ by omitting the $i$th entry. This gives rise to the diagram
       \begin{equation}
         \begin{tikzcd}
	{[0]} & {[1]} & {[2]} & \cdots
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift left=4, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift right=4, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow["\cdots"{description}, no head, from=1-3, to=1-4]
\end{tikzcd}.
       \end{equation}
       \item $\sigma^n_i: [n+1] \to [n]$ for $i \in [n]$ is a surjective function such that $\sigma_i(i) = \sigma_i(i+1)$. This defines a diagram
       \begin{equation}
          \begin{tikzcd}
	{[0]} & {[1]} & {[2]} & \cdots
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\cdots"{description}, no head, from=1-4, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}.
       \end{equation}
   \end{enumerate}
   The arrows $\{\delta_i^n,\sigma_i^n \}$ together generate the diagram
   \begin{equation}\label{eq:cosimplicial-diagram}
       \begin{tikzcd}
	{[0]} & {[1]} & {[2]} & \cdots
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow[from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift right=4, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift left=4, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\cdots"{description}, no head, from=1-4, to=1-3]
\end{tikzcd}
   \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{app:def:simplicial-cosimplicial-object}

A \textit{simplicial object} $\mathscr{X}_{\bullet}$ in $\textbf{H}$ is a functor
\begin{equation}
    \mathscr{X}_{\bullet}: \boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op} \to \textbf{H}.
\end{equation}

A \textit{co-simplicial object} in $\textbf{H}$ is a functor
\begin{equation}
     \mathscr{X}_{\bullet}: \boldsymbol{\Delta} \to \textbf{H}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{app:def:groupoid-object}
    A \textit{groupoid object} ${\mathscr G}_{\bullet}$ in \textbf{H} is a simplicial object ${\mathscr G}_{\bullet}: \boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op}\to \textbf{H}$ such that for every $n\geq 0$ and every pair of subsets $S,S'\subseteq[n]$ with
    \begin{equation}
        S\cup S'=[n],\qquad S\cap S'=\{s\},
    \end{equation}
    the square
    \begin{equation}\label{app:eq:segal}
        \begin{tikzcd}
	{\mathscr G_{[n]}} && {\mathscr G_{S}} \\
	\\
	{\mathscr G_{S'}} && {\mathscr G_{\{s\}}}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=1-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}
    \end{equation}
    is Cartesian, where $\mathscr G_S$ denotes $\mathscr G_{[|S|-1]}$ via the unique order-preserving bijection $[|S|-1]\cong S$, and all maps are induced by the inclusions of subsets (cf.\ \cite[Proposition 6.1.2.6]{lurie-htt}).
    
    Imposing this only for initial and final segments $S=\{0,\dots,k\}$, $S'=\{k,\dots,n\}$ is the Segal condition, which characterizes category objects. The general condition additionally encodes invertibility. The $\infty$-category of groupoid objects in $\textbf{H}$ is denoted ${\rm Grpd}(\textbf{H})$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
The functor
\begin{equation}
    {\rm Cnst}(*)_{\bullet}: \boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op} \to \textbf{H}
\end{equation}
constant at $* \in {\rm ob\, }\textbf{H}$, the terminal object in $\textbf{H}$, is a groupoid object. It is furthermore the terminal object in ${\rm Grpd}(\textbf{H})$.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{app:def:gp-obj}
  A \textit{group object} $(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G})_{\bullet}$ in $\textbf{H}$ is a groupoid object $(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G})_{\bullet}$ that is pointed in ${\rm Grpd}(\textbf{H})$, meaning it is equipped with a morphism
  \begin{equation}
      {\rm pt}: {\rm Cnst}(*)_{\bullet} \to \left(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G}\right)_{\bullet}
  \end{equation}
  such that the component of $[0]\in {\rm ob\,}\boldsymbol{\Delta}$ is an equivalence
  \begin{equation}
      (\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G})_{0} \cong {\rm Cnst}(*)_{0} = *.
  \end{equation}
We denote the collection of group objects in \textbf{H} as
\begin{equation}
    {\rm Grp}(\textbf{H}) \to {\rm Grpd}(\textbf{H}).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- remark-38: body_md -->
\label{app:rmk:stacky-gp}
In the main text, we speak of stacky groups as objects $\mathcal{G}$ in $\textbf{H}$. These are obtained from group objects as in Definition~\ref{app:def:gp-obj} by first computing the homotopy colimit of the diagram defined by the image of the reversed $\{\delta_i^n,\sigma_i^n\}$ maps in $\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op}$
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{B}\mathcal{G} := {\rm hocolim}\left(\begin{tikzcd}
	{\left(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G}\right)_0} & {\left(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G}\right)_1} & {\left(\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G}\right)_2} & \cdots
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-2, to=1-1]
	\arrow[shift left=2, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[shift right=2, from=1-2, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift left=4, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow[shift right=4, from=1-3, to=1-2]
	\arrow["\cdots"{description}, no head, from=1-3, to=1-4]
\end{tikzcd} \right),
\end{equation}
and then computing the loop space as the pullback
\begin{equation}
    \begin{tikzcd}
	\mathcal{G} && {*} \\
	\\
	{*} && {\mathbf{B}\mathcal{G}}
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=1-3]
	\arrow[from=1-1, to=3-1]
	\arrow["\lrcorner"{anchor=center, pos=0.125}, draw=none, from=1-1, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=1-3, to=3-3]
	\arrow[from=3-1, to=3-3]
\end{tikzcd}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-38 -->

<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
\label{app:def:n-truncation}
 For $n\geq -2$, there exist \textit{$n$-truncation} functors
 \begin{equation}\label{eq:n-truncation-h}
     \tau_{\leq n}: \textbf{H} \to {\rm Sh}\left({\rm CartSp},n{\rm Grpd}\right) \hookrightarrow\textbf{H},
 \end{equation}
left adjoint to the inclusion of $n$-truncated objects (Definition~\ref{app:def:n-truncated}). Concretely, $\tau_{\leq n}X$ is obtained by applying the $n$-truncation \eqref{eq:truncation-groupoids} objectwise, $U\mapsto\tau_{\leq n}(X(U))$, followed by $\infty$-sheafification. The resulting evaluations $\tau_{\leq n}X(U)$ are $n$-groupoids.

The functors \eqref{eq:n-truncation-h} are reflective and preserve finite products \cite[Proposition 5.1.49]{Schreiber:2013pra}, \cite[Proposition 5.5.6.18, Lemma 6.5.1.2]{lurie-htt}.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
\label{app:def:n-truncated}
   A smooth stack $X\in {\rm ob}\, \textbf{H}$ is said to be \textit{$n$-truncated} if all evaluations $X(U)$ are $n$-groupoids (included as $\infty$-groupoids with only trivial morphisms for $d>n$).

   The $n$-truncation $\tau_{\leq n}X$ of any stack is clearly an $n$-truncated object of \textbf{H}.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
\label{app:def:n-connected}
An object $X\in {\rm ob\,} \textbf{H}$ is called \textit{$n$-connected} if its $n$-truncation is contractible 
\begin{equation}
    \tau_{\leq n}X \cong *
\end{equation}
 e.g. \cite[Definition 5.1.104]{Schreiber:2013pra}, cf. \cite[Section 6.5.1]{lurie-htt}.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- definition-18: body_md -->
\label{app:def:n-connected-cover}
For an object $X \in {\rm ob}\, \textbf{H}$ that is pointed, its \textit{$n$-connected cover} $X\langle n \rangle$ is defined as the homotopy fiber of the canonical projection map to its $n$-truncation $\tau_{\leq n}X$ \cite[Definition 5.2.22]{Schreiber:2013pra}
\begin{equation}
    X\langle n \rangle := {\rm hofib}\left( \eta: X \to \tau_{\leq n}X\right).
\end{equation}
By construction, the cover $X \langle n \rangle$ is an $n$-connected object in \textbf{H}.
<!-- end definition-18 -->
<!-- definition-19: body_md -->
\label{app:def:n-truncated-connected-morphism}
A morphism $f: X \to Y$, regarded as an object of the slice topos $\textbf{H}_{/Y}$ (whose terminal object is $\mathrm{id}_Y$), is called:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textit{$n$-truncated} if it is $n$-truncated as an object of $\textbf{H}_{/Y}$, i.e.\ its homotopy fibers are $n$-truncated \cite[Definition 2.58]{Sati:2020ovu}, cf. \cite[Definition 5.5.6.8]{lurie-htt}
    \begin{equation}
        \tau_{\leq n}(f) \cong f \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}_{/Y},
    \end{equation}
    \item \textit{$n$-connected} if its homotopy fibers are $(n-1)$-connected (Definition~\ref{app:def:n-connected}), i.e.
    \begin{equation}
        \tau_{\leq n-1}(f) \cong \mathrm{id}_Y \in {\rm ob\,}\textbf{H}_{/Y}.
    \end{equation}
    Here, we are using the convention (e.g.\ \cite[Section 4.1]{hatcher2002algebraic}) under which the Postnikov projection $\tau_{\leq n+1}X \to \tau_{\leq n}X$ is $(n+1)$-connected. In the indexing of \cite[Section 6.5.1]{lurie-htt}, an $n$-connected morphism is \textit{$n$-connective}.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-19 -->
<!-- definition-20: body_md -->
\label{app:def:cohesive} The
\textit{cohesive structure} on \textbf{H} consists of a collection of adjoint functors
\begin{equation}
\begin{tikzcd}
    \mathbf{H} \ar[rrr, "{\mathrm{Shp}}"{description, name=shp}, yshift=4.5ex]
    \ar[rrr, "{\mathrm{Pnt}}"{description, name=pnt}, yshift=-1.5ex]
     &&& \infty\mathrm{Grpd} \ar[lll, "{\mathrm{Dsc}}"{description, name=dsc}, yshift=1.5ex]
     \ar[lll, "{\mathrm{Cht}}"{description, name=cht}, yshift=-4.5ex]
     \arrow[phantom, from=shp, to=dsc, "\dashv" rotate=-90, no line]
     \arrow[phantom, from=dsc, to=pnt, "\dashv" rotate=-90, no line]
     \arrow[phantom, from=pnt, to=cht, "\dashv" rotate=-90, no line]
\end{tikzcd},
\end{equation}
which can be understood as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $\rm Shp: \textbf{H} \to \infty{\rm Grpd}$, the \textit{shape} functor, extracts the bare homotopy type of a smooth $\infty$-groupoid,
    \item $\rm Dsc: \infty{\rm Grpd}\to \textbf{H}$, the \textit{discrete} functor, embeds an $\infty$-groupoid as a smooth $\infty$-groupoid equipped with the \textit{discrete} topology,
    \item $\rm Pnt: \textbf{H} \to \infty{\rm Grpd}$, the \textit{points} functor, also called the \textit{global sections} functor, extracts the value of a smooth $\infty$-groupoid at the point,
    \item $\rm Cht: \infty{\rm Grpd}\to \textbf{H}$, the \textit{chaotic} functor, also called \textit{codiscrete}, embeds an $\infty$-groupoid as a smooth $\infty$-groupoid equipped with the \textit{co-discrete} topology.
\end{enumerate}

This set of adjoint functors gives rise to the \textit{shape}, \textit{flat}, and \textit{sharp adjoint modalities} on \textbf{H}
\begin{equation}
    \sharp \vdash \flat \vdash 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
: \textbf{H} \to \textbf{H},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
    
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
:= \mathrm{Dsc}\circ \mathrm{Shp}, \quad \flat:= \mathrm{Dsc} \circ \mathrm{Pnt}, \quad \sharp:= \mathrm{Cht}\circ \mathrm{Pnt},
\end{equation}
 respectively encoding the pure shape, pure discrete, and pure continuous (or pure cohesive) aspects of a higher smooth stack. These endofunctors are idempotent \cite[Proposition 8.1.45]{SatiSchreiber2026}.
<!-- end definition-20 -->
<!-- definition-21: body_md -->
\label{app:def:discrete}
    A stack $X$ is called \textit{discrete} if it is in the essential image of the discrete functor ${\rm Dsc}:{\infty \rm Grpd}\to \textbf{H}$. 
    
    Therefore, for any stack $Y$, the objects $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 Y, \flat Y$ are discrete stacks.
<!-- end definition-21 -->
<!-- remark-39: body_md -->
The image $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X$ of a stack $X \in {\rm ob}(\textbf{H})$ under the $
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
$-modality is the discrete inclusion of the underlying homotopy type of $X$, which may be understood as the path $\infty$-groupoid $\Pi_{\infty}\vert X \vert$ of the geometric realization $\vert X \vert$ (a topological space) of $X$. One may furthermore ask how to construct the \textit{smooth} path $\infty$-groupoid $\mathcal{P}_{\infty}X$ of $X$. While the latter has a natural definition, one can show (e.g. \cite[Proposition 4.3.49]{Sati_Schreiber_2026}) that these two are equivalent as objects in \textbf{H}.
<!-- end remark-39 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{app:prop:counits}
Let \textbf{H} be a cohesive topos. The (co)unit maps
\begin{equation}\label{app:eq:counits}
    \eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_X: X \to 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X, \quad \varepsilon^{\flat}_X:\flat X \to X
\end{equation}
induce the following equivalences of \textit{external} hom-$\infty$-groupoids, for $Y$ a \textit{discrete} object 
\begin{equation}
  \textbf{H}(
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X, Y) \xrightarrow{\cong} \textbf{H}(X,Y), \quad \textbf{H}(Y,\flat X) \xrightarrow{\cong} \textbf{H}(Y,X).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- definition-22: body_md -->
\label{app:def:pts-to-piec} For \textbf{H} as in Definition~\ref{app:def:cohesive}, the (co)unit transformations of $\flat,
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
:\textbf{H}\to \textbf{H}$ induce the \textit{points-to-pieces transform} of any object $X\in \mathrm{ob}(\textbf{H})$, defined as the following composition
\begin{equation}
    \flat X \xrightarrow{\varepsilon_X^{\flat}} X \xrightarrow{\eta^{
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\scriptsize\textesh}
}_X} 
  \raisebox{1pt}{\rm\normalfont\textesh}
 X.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-22 -->
<!-- definition-23: body_md -->
An $\infty$-category $\mathcal{C}$ is called \textit{stable} if it satisfies the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item it has a zero object, meaning an object $0 \in \mathrm{ob}\,\mathcal{C}$ which is both initial and terminal (cf. \cite[Definition 1.1.1.1]{lurie2017higher}),
    \item every morphism admits a fiber and cofiber,
    \item a diagram $X \to Y \to Z$ is a fiber sequence iff it is a cofiber sequence.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-23 -->
<!-- definition-24: body_md -->
For $\mathcal{C}$ an $\infty$-category with finite limits, let $\mathcal{C}_{*/}$ be its $\infty$-category of pointed objects, and $\Omega: \mathcal{C}_{*/} \to \mathcal{C}_{*/}$ the \textit{loop} functor, defined on objects as the pullback $\Omega((X,x)) = * \times_{X}*$. The \textit{$\infty$-category of spectrum objects} is the limit (cf. \cite[Remark 1.4.2.9, Proposition 1.4.2.24]{lurie2017higher})
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C}) := \varprojlim \left( \cdots \xrightarrow{\Omega} \mathcal{C}_{*/} \xrightarrow{\Omega} \mathcal{C}_{*/} \xrightarrow{\Omega} \mathcal{C}_{*/} \right).
\end{equation}
In particular, a \textit{spectrum object} $E \in \mathrm{ob\,}\mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$ can be described as a collection of pointed objects $\{E_i\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ together with equivalences
\begin{equation}
    E_n \xrightarrow{\sim} \Omega E_{n+1}.
\end{equation}
It is a stable $\infty$-category \cite[Proposition 1.4.2.11]{lurie2017higher}.
<!-- end definition-24 -->
<!-- remark-40: body_md -->
For $\textbf{H} = \mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{CartSp}, \infty\mathrm{Grpd})$, its category of spectrum objects is equivalently
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}) = \mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{CartSp},\mathrm{Sp}),
\end{equation}
sheaves on the site of Cartesian spaces valued in stabilized spaces (spectra), since $\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}) = \textbf{H}\otimes \mathrm{Sp}$, using the fact that \textbf{H} is presentable and that $\mathrm{Sh(CartSp,-)}$ is a left-exact localization of presheaves.
<!-- end remark-40 -->
<!-- remark-41: body_md -->
For $X \in \mathrm{ob\,Sp}(\mathcal{C})$, $X[n]$ denotes the image of $X$ under the suspension functor $\Sigma: \mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})\to \mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$ applied $n$ times, inverse equivalence to the loop functor $\Omega: \mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})\to \mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$. If $n<0$, this is instead the image under the iterated application of the loop functor.
<!-- end remark-41 -->
<!-- definition-25: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{ho}\mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$ be the triangulated homotopy category of $\mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$. A $\mathrm{t}$\textit{-structure} on $\mathrm{Sp}(\mathcal{C})$ is a $\mathrm{t}$-structure on $\mathcal{D}$, which consists of a pair of full subcategories ${\mathcal{D}}_{\leq 0}, \mathcal{D}_{\geq 0}$, each stable under isomorphism, such that
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
    \item For objects $X$ in $\mathcal{D}_{\geq 0}$, $Y$ in $\mathcal{D}_{\leq 0}$, it holds that
    \begin{equation}
        \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(X, Y[-1]) = 0.
    \end{equation}
    \item There are inclusions $\mathcal{D}_{\geq0}[1] \subset \mathcal{D}_{\geq 0}$, $\mathcal{D}_{\leq0}[-1] \subset \mathcal{D}_{\leq 0}$.

\item For any $X \in \mathrm{ob\,}\mathcal{D}$, there are objects $X' \in \mathrm{ob\,}\mathcal{D}_{\geq 0}$ and $X'' \in \mathrm{ob\,}\mathcal{D}_{\leq 0}[-1]$ fitting in a distinguished triangle
\begin{equation}
    X' \to X \to X''.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
 This defines categories $\mathcal{D}_{\geq n} = \mathcal{D}_{\geq 0}[n]$ and $\mathcal{D}_{\leq n} = \mathcal{D}_{\leq 0}[n]$ for all $n$.
<!-- end definition-25 -->
<!-- remark-42: body_md -->
Roughly speaking, a $\mathrm{t}$-structure allows us to do homological algebra.
<!-- end remark-42 -->
<!-- definition-26: body_md -->
\label{app:def:truncation-functors-spec}
There is a standard non-degenerate $\mathrm{t}$-structure on $\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})$ defined through sheaf homotopy groups (\cite[Proposition 1.4.3.4]{lurie2017higher}, and using the hypercompleteness of \textbf{H} cf. \cite[Section 6.5]{lurie-htt}). This defines $\infty$-subcategories $\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\geq n}$, $\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\leq n}$, whose homotopy categories are the corresponding $\mathrm{ho}\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})$-subcategories. The inclusions
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\geq n} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}),\quad \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\leq n} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}) 
\end{equation}
have right and left adjoint functors, respectively,
\begin{equation}
    \tau_{\geq n}:\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}) \to \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\geq n}, \quad \tau_{\leq n}: \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H}) \to \mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\leq n},
\end{equation}
called \textit{truncation functors}.
<!-- end definition-26 -->
<!-- definition-27: body_md -->
\label{app:def:conn-spec}
The subcategory $\mathrm{Sp}(\textbf{H})_{\geq 0}$ is the category of \textit{connective spectrum objects}, also denoted as $\mathrm{Sp}^{\rm cn}(\textbf{H})$, which have the property that their \textit{sheaf} homotopy groups vanish as follows:
\begin{equation}
    \underline{\pi_{-n}}(E) := \underline{\pi_0}(E_n)=0, \quad n>0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-27 -->
<!-- remark-43: body_md -->
\label{app:rmk:equivalence-einfty-connective}
Roughly speaking, a grouplike $E_{\infty}$ object in \textbf{H} is an object $E$ equipped with a composition law
\begin{equation}
    \otimes: E\times E \to E
\end{equation}
that is invertible and coherently commutative (technically, it is a grouplike algebra over the $E_{\infty}$-operad, see \cite[Section 5.2]{lurie2017higher}). These objects form a category $\mathrm{Grp}_{E_{\infty}}(\textbf{H})$. There is an equivalence
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Grp}_{E_{\infty}}(\textbf{H}) \cong \mathrm{Sp}^{\rm cn}(\textbf{H})
\end{equation}
with the category of connective spectrum objects in \textbf{H}. It is shown that grouplike $E_{\infty}$ objects admit infinitely many deloopings, which are the ones used to construct the corresponding connective spectrum object. This makes use of the bar construction, see \cite[Sections 5.2.2.1--5.2.2.7]{lurie2017higher}.
<!-- end remark-43 -->
<!-- definition-28: body_md -->
\label{app:def:dold-kan}
Let $\mathcal{C} = \mathrm{Sh}({\mathrm{CartSp,Ab}})$ be the category of sheaves on Cartesian spaces valued in abelian $1$-groups.

There is an equivalence
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Fun}(\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op}, \mathcal{C}) \cong \mathrm{Ch}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{C})
\end{equation}
between the category of simplicial objects in $\cal C$ (cf. Definition~\ref{app:def:simplicial-cosimplicial-object}), and the category of chain complexes in $\mathcal{C}$. These equivalences are canonically realized by the \textit{normalization} $N$ and denormalization (\textit{Dold--Kan}) $\rm DK$ functors
\begin{equation}
    N:\mathrm{Fun}(\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op}, \mathcal{C}) \to \mathrm{Ch}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{C}), \quad \mathrm{DK}: \mathrm{Ch}_{\geq 0}(\mathcal{C}) \to \mathrm{Fun}(\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\rm op}, \mathcal{C}).
\end{equation}
Informally, $N$ removes degenerate simplices by intersecting kernels, and compresses all simplicial maps into a single map, stagewise, the differential, while $\mathrm{DK}$ generates back the degenerate simplices freely and constructs the boundary maps from the differential.

Applying $\mathrm{DK}$ objectwise and passing to underlying simplicial sets yields a functor
\begin{equation}
    \mathrm{Ch}_{\geq 0}\left(\mathrm{Sh}(\mathrm{CartSp},\mathrm{Ab})\right)\longrightarrow \mathrm{Fun}\left(\mathrm{CartSp}^{\rm op},\infty\mathrm{Grpd}\right),
\end{equation}
which sends objectwise quasi-isomorphisms to objectwise equivalences, and objectwise homology to objectwise homotopy groups, $\pi_k\,\mathrm{DK}(C)(U)\cong H_k(C(U))$. Its values are objects of $\textbf{H}$ (after sheafification if necessary).
<!-- end definition-28 -->
<!-- remark-44: body_md -->
\label{app:rmk:hz-modules}
The integers $\mathbb{Z}$, as a discrete commutative ring object in $\mathbf{H}$, define an \textit{Eilenberg--MacLane ring spectrum} $H\mathbb{Z} \in \mathrm{CAlg}(\mathrm{Sp}(\mathbf{H}))_{\ge 0}$. The stable $\infty$-category of $H\mathbb{Z}$-module spectra $\mathrm{Mod}_{H\mathbb{Z}}(\mathrm{Sp}(\mathbf{H}))$ is equivalent to the unbounded derived $\infty$-category $\mathrm{Sh(CartSp},\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z}))$ of abelian sheaves in $\mathbf{H}$, under which connective $H\mathbb{Z}$-modules correspond to the connective $\mathrm{Sh(CartSp},\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{Z}))_{\geq 0}$. Technically, this uses the hypercompleteness of \textbf{H}.
<!-- end remark-44 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{pin:coeff}
For $0\leq s\leq4$, the group cohomology of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ with coefficients in $A^\pm$ is
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{c|ccccc}
$s$ & $0$ & $1$ & $2$ & $3$ & $4$\\ \midrule
$H^s(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)$ & $A$ & $\mathbb{Z}_2$ & $0$ & $\mathbb{Z}_2$ & $0$\\
$H^s(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^-)$ & $\mathbb{Z}_2$ & $0$ & $\mathbb{Z}_2$ & $0$ & $\mathbb{Z}_2$
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The exponential sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}^\varepsilon\to\mathbb{R}^\varepsilon\to A^\varepsilon\to0$ is exact and
equivariant. Since $\mathbb{R}$ is a $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space, $H^s(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{R}^\varepsilon)=0$ for $s\geq1$, and moreover $H^0(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{R}^-)=0$. The associated long exact sequence therefore gives $H^s(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^\varepsilon)\cong
H^{s+1}(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^\varepsilon)$ for $s\geq1$, and $H^0(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^-)\cong H^1(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)=\mathbb{Z}_2$. Concretely,
$H^0(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^-)=\{f\in U(1):f^2=1\}=\{\pm1\}$. Finally, $H^0(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)=A$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{pin:fminus}
The map $f_-\colon\mathbb{Z}^-\to A^+$, $a\mapsto(-1)^a$, is equivariant, and
$(f_-)_*\colon H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)\to H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)$ is an isomorphism $\mathbb{Z}_2\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
Equivariance holds since $(-1)^{-a}=(-1)^a$. We factor $f_-=j\circ r$, where $r\colon\mathbb{Z}^-\to\mathbb{Z}_2$ is reduction mod $2$, which is equivariant since $-1\equiv1\pmod2$, and $j\colon\mathbb{Z}_2=\{\pm1\}\hookrightarrow A^+$ is the inclusion.

The short exact sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}^-\xrightarrow{2}\mathbb{Z}^-\xrightarrow{r}\mathbb{Z}_2\to0$ gives the exact sequence
\begin{equation}
    H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)\xrightarrow{r_*}H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}_2)\to H^4(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)=0.
\end{equation}
Multiplication by $2$ vanishes on $H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}^-)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$, so $r_*$ is an isomorphism.

Since $A$ is divisible, the sequence $0\to\mathbb{Z}_2\xrightarrow{j}A^+\xrightarrow{(\cdot)^2}A^+\to0$ is exact, and it gives the exact sequence
\begin{equation}
    0=H^2(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)\to H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,\mathbb{Z}_2)\xrightarrow{j_*}H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)\xrightarrow{\,2\,}H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+).
\end{equation}
Multiplication by $2$ vanishes on $H^3(\mathbb{Z}_2,A^+)\cong\mathbb{Z}_2$, so $j_*$ is an isomorphism.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
